sens: Fragment of a millstone
Detached part, slice or portion of something
Half of a fruit or a round shape
H6400.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a piece of a millstone, that large round stone that grinds grain. In Judges 9:53, a woman throws a piece of a millstone on Abimelech's head from a tower, killing him: it is a heavy and deadly object. The same story is recalled in 2 Samuel 11:21.
2. The word also more broadly refers to a portion or a slice detached from something. In 1 Samuel 30:12, a hungry man is given a piece of dried figs and raisins to restore him: it is a portion of food that can be held in the hand.
3. It can mean a half, an equal part of a divided thing. In Song of Solomon 4:3 and 6:7, the cheek of the beloved is compared to a half of a pomegranate: it is an image of beauty and symmetry. Job 41:15 speaks of the heart of Leviathan as hard as the lower millstone, the fixed stone of the mill.
H6400.origine: The Hebrew word pelach comes from a root meaning "to split, divide, cleave." It refers to the idea of separating, cutting into parts. The millstone was indeed made up of two stone disks that separated from one another: the idea of division and fracture is at the heart of the word. That is why pelach can refer both to a detached piece and a half.
H6400.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. It first appears in a context of violence: Judges 9:53 and 2 Samuel 11:21 mention the piece of millstone that kills Abimelech, a wartime event. In 1 Samuel 30:12, it describes a portion of food in a context of survival and rescue. In Job 41:15, it characterizes a stone, a symbol of hardness. Finally, in Song of Solomon 4:3 and 6:7, it represents a half of a pomegranate to express the beauty of the beloved. The word thus oscillates between the concrete idea of a fragment or a half, and figurative or poetic uses.
H6400.portee: This word reminds us that everyday objects, even as ordinary as a millstone or a piece of fruit, can become powerful images in the Bible: symbols of death or beauty, strength or nourishment. For the believer, this shows how every detail of material and visible life points to deeper spiritual realities.

sens: Leader of the Israelite people during the time of Nehemiah
H6401.detail: Pilcha is a man who lived at the time of the return from exile, after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:24, among the leaders of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah to commit to obeying the Law of Moses. His name appears in a list of representatives of Israel who publicly acknowledged their commitment to God.
H6401.origine: The name Pilcha literally means "to cut" or "to split." It is a Hebrew name among the Israelite leaders of the return from exile in the fifth century B.C.
H6401.emploi: Pilcha appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:24. He is included in the solemn list of the leaders of the people who affixed their seal to the covenant document that Nehemiah established after the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem. This presence in the official record shows that he was a man of responsibility and authority among the Israelites who returned from exile.

sens: Work or function performed in the service of a god or a temple
Set of acts and objects dedicated to divine worship
H6402.detail:
1. Service refers to the work or function one fulfills for God, particularly the worship rendered in the temple. It is the work of the priests and Levites, who take care of God's house and everything related to it. In Ezra 7:19, it refers to the service of the temple in Jerusalem: the utensils given to Ezra were used to carry out this daily worship.
2. By extension, the word evokes the entirety of acts of worship and sacred objects that make up this service: sacrifices, prayers, the maintenance of the temple, everything that concretely honors God in His holy place.
H6402.origine: The word comes from an Aramaic root meaning "to work, to serve." It is related to terms that denote work or service in general, but here specifically applied to religious service. This root reflects the idea that divine worship is a form of work, a task that requires dedication and regularity.
H6402.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 7:19. In this context, King Artaxerxes entrusts Ezra with precious utensils — bowls, cups, plates of gold and silver — intended for the service of the temple in Jerusalem. This passage underscores the religious and political importance of this service: everything necessary for worship must be in place and properly maintained for the temple to fulfill its holy function.
H6402.portee: This entry reminds us that worship rendered to God is never a purely spiritual or immaterial act: it requires tools, concrete gestures, organization, and dedication. The service of the temple thus symbolizes the work that each believer accomplishes for God in their life, with seriousness and faithfulness.

sens: to escape, to save from danger
to pull someone from danger, to put them in safety
one who delivers, who saves
H6403.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of fleeing, of escaping: to get away from a threat. In Psalms 17:13, the psalmist asks God to "deliver" him from the wicked — it is about not being harmed by the enemy.
2. Next, it is the action of saving someone in danger: putting them to safety, pulling them from a situation that threatens their life. In Psalms 22:5, the psalmist remembers that "you delivered them," our fathers — God rescued them from their perils.
3. Thirdly, it is one who fulfills this role of savior, protector. In 2 Samuel 22:2 and Psalms 40:18, the word is translated as "deliverer" to refer to God Himself, or the person who comes to the rescue. It is the figure who delivers, the savior.
H6403.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of slipping away, escaping, thus getting out of reach. The Piel (intensive form) marks the action of making someone escape, putting them in safety, while the agent noun naturally derives: one who liberates. The word also appears in Aramaic in the same sense.
H6403.emploi: This verb is used 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms (where it appears nearly 15 times) and in historical narratives. It often describes the salvation that God brings to His people in the face of their enemies (2 Samuel 22:44) or evil (Psalms 31:2). The word can refer to the act of saving itself, or to the one who saves. In Isaiah 5:29, it is even used for a wild beast that carries off its prey. It is a word of appeal and trust: one asks God to "deliver" those who call upon Him (Psalms 37:40).
H6403.portee: This word speaks to the very heart of biblical faith: God is the deliverer of His people. For the believer going through trials, it is a word of hope: there is someone who can pull them from evil and put them in safety. The psalmists who use it continually teach to pray without giving up, to call for help from the one who has the power to save. It is also a name given to Jesus Christ in Christian faith: He is the Deliverer par excellence.

sens: Member of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
Son of Jahdaï and descendant of Caleb
H6404G.detail: 1. Péleth is a man from the tribe of Judah who lived during the period of the divided monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, which shows that he did not play a major role in the history of Israel. 2. Péleth is the son of Jahdaï and a descendant of Caleb, an important figure in the Old Testament. He is part of a genealogical family from the tribe of Judah: he had brothers named Reguem, Jotham, Guéschan, Épha, and Schaaph, as shown in 1 Chronicles 2:47.
H6404G.origine: The name Péleth means "deliverance" in Hebrew. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of escaping, saving oneself, or being preserved from danger. This name reflects the faith of Jewish families, who placed their hope for protection and salvation in God. Like many Hebrew names, it expresses a prayer or testimony: parents would give a name with spiritual significance to their child.
H6404G.emploi: Péleth appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:47, where he is listed in the genealogy of Caleb. This passage enumerates the children of Jahdaï, among whom is Péleth. The genealogy tells us nothing else about his life, deeds, or importance. He represents one of those many ancestors whose name has been preserved in the genealogical records of Israel, but whose personal story is not told.

sens: Warrior of Israel who joined David at Ziklag
Son of Azmaveth and brother of Jeziel
H6404H.detail: Péleth is a warrior from the time of the divided monarchy. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:3, where he is listed among the valiant warriors who came to join David at Ziklag. His father is Azmaveth, and his brother is named Jeziel. The name "Péleth" means "deliverance" in Hebrew, which reflects Israel's trust in God's liberating power.
H6404H.origine: The name Péleth comes from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of escaping, evading danger, or being saved. This term refers to deliverance, to divine protection in the face of threats. Azmaveth's father also appears in the genealogies of Israel, and this surname denotes a family engaged in the battles of the kingdom.
H6404H.emploi: Péleth is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 12:3. He is a military leader who joined David's troops at Ziklag, at the time when David was gathering his warriors before becoming king. This mention places him among David's faithful heroes, those who recognized his royal legitimacy and committed themselves to him. His inclusion in this list of valiant warriors shows that he was a renowned and trusted warrior.
H6404H.portee: Péleth embodies loyalty to the king chosen by God. His rallying to David at Ziklag, while David was fleeing Saul, shows how faithful warriors followed the one they recognized as the true leader according to God's plan. This example encourages the reader to remain faithful to the promises and leaders that God establishes.

sens: The act of escaping from danger, distress, or death
H6405.detail: 1. Deliverance is the state of one who has escaped from great peril. In Psalm 32, the psalmist thanks God for surrounding him "with songs of deliverance" — that is, cries of joy that celebrate the escape from distress and anguish. It is the relief and victory of salvation.
H6405.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to escape" or "to save." It properly designates the act of fleeing or pulling away from danger, and by extension, the result of that act — the state of being safe. This is why it is used to speak of God's help, which rescues His people from danger.
H6405.emploi: This word appears once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 32:7. It is used to describe the songs that God inspires — hymns of gratitude that express the joy of one whom He has saved from distress. It is a term of jubilation and praise.
H6405.portee: Deliverance reminds us that salvation is not a mere abstract forgiveness: it is a concrete, joyful liberation, that of a person who cried out for help and whom God pulled from the pit. This word invites the believer to express gratitude through songs and to recognize God as their personal savior.

sens: Son of Raphu, spy sent by Moses
Representative of the tribe of Benjamin during the first reconnaissance of Canaan
H6406G.detail: 1. Palthi is the name of a man chosen among the twelve representatives of the tribes of Israel to explore the land of Canaan before entering Israel. He is explicitly designated as coming from the tribe of Benjamin and as the son of Raphu (Numbers 13:9). He is part of this first reconnaissance mission that Moses sends to evaluate the promised land. 2. His role in the biblical narrative is limited to this single mention in Numbers: he is one of the twelve spies who go to explore Canaan. Although we do not know the details of his report or his vote upon return, he represents the tribe of Benjamin in this historic mission of Israel.
H6406G.origine: The name Palthi means "my deliverance" or "my escape" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing flight or deliverance. It is a theophoric name that expresses trust in God's protection and deliverance. The name reflects the faith of the parents in the Lord's ability to liberate and save.
H6406G.emploi: Palthi is a minor historical figure, mentioned only once in the Bible in the book of Numbers. He is presented in the context of the selection of the twelve spies that Moses sends to explore the land of Canaan (Numbers 13). He represents his tribe, Benjamin, in this important delegation. After this reconnaissance mission, his name completely disappears from biblical accounts. He belongs to the early events in the desert, at the time when Israel is about to take possession of the promised land.
H6406G.portee: Palthi reminds us that the small players in biblical history play their role in God's grand plan. Although we know nothing more about him, his participation in the reconnaissance of Canaan places him at a pivotal moment in Israel's history. His name, meaning "my deliverance," invites us to consider that every believer can trust God to lead them toward the fulfillment of His promises.

sens: Man living during the united monarchy, son of Laish
H6406H.detail: Palthi is a man from the time of David and Saul. He is the son of Laish and a resident of Gallim. King Saul gave him his daughter Michal in marriage, although Michal was already David's wife. This episode shows how Saul sought to distance David from his family by giving her to another man. Later, the same man is called Paltiel (a variant of the same name), indicating that Palthi and Paltiel refer to the same person with slightly different spellings in Hebrew.
H6406H.origine: The name Palthi means "my deliverance" in Hebrew, composed of elements evoking the idea of escaping or being saved. Its equivalent Paltiel (Paltiel instead of Palthi) is another form of the same name, used in other biblical passages to refer to the same person.
H6406H.emploi: Palthi appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Samuel 25:44, where he is identified as the man to whom King Saul gave Michal in marriage. Michal, daughter of Saul and David's first wife, was separated from David and given to Palthi at the king's pleasure. This action shows Saul's desire to break the bond between David and his house. The same character is referred to elsewhere by the name Paltiel, revealing that the names Palthi and Paltiel are two forms of the same Hebrew name.

sens: Warrior of Israel during the time of David, leader of one of the twelve monthly divisions of the royal army
H6407.detail: 1. Péleth is a military officer in the service of King David, responsible for one of the twelve divisions that made up the permanent army of the kingdom, each commanded in turn for one month of the year (2 Samuel 23:26).
H6407.origine: The name Péleth means "the one who escapes" or "deliverance" in Hebrew, likely formed from a root evoking the idea of flight or rescue. He may be a descendant of an ancestor named Palti or a person from the place Beth-Palet. The name belongs to the family of theophoric names from the Israelite royal period.
H6407.emploi: Péleth appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:26, in the list of David's thirty elite warriors. He is mentioned as "Ira, son of Ikkesh, of Tekoa," to whom the title of "chief of the division of the twelfth month" is associated. His inclusion in this list of the king David's renowned warriors attests to his military importance and loyalty to the royal cause.

sens: priest at the time of the return from exile
H6408.detail: Pilthaï is a Jewish priest who lived at the time of the return from exile, after the destruction of the temple in Jerusalem by Babylon. He represented the priestly house of Moadia (Nehemiah 12:17) — that is, he was the chief or leader among those who returned with Zerubbabel to rebuild the temple.
H6408.origine: The name Pilthaï literally means "my deliverances" in Hebrew, formed from the root that evokes escape or salvation. It is a meaningful name that recalls the deliverance from Babylonian exile, a central theme of this restoration period.
H6408.emploi: Pilthaï appears only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 12:17. He is mentioned in a list of priests and heads of priestly families who returned from captivity with Zerubbabel to resume temple worship. This list establishes the order and legitimacy of the new leaders of divine service in Jerusalem.
H6408.portee: The name of Pilthaï reminds us that the return from exile was not a dramatic event but a humble and administrative restoration: God preserved the people, brought back His priests, and reorganized worship. Even a minor character like Pilthaï, of whom we know nothing else, represents God's faithfulness to rebuild His people.

sens: Prince of Issachar responsible for dividing the land of Canaan
H6409G.detail: Paltiel is a leader of Israel, son of Azzan, designated as one of the twelve princes responsible for dividing the territory of Canaan among the tribes after the conquest. His name means "God delivers" in Hebrew. He represents the tribe of Issachar in this important mission of organizing the promised land (Numbers 34:26).
H6409G.origine: The name Paltiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Pal" (to deliver, to escape) and "El" (God). It literally means "God delivers." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in God's saving action.
H6409G.emploi: Paltiel appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 34:26, where he is identified as the prince of Issachar among the twelve representatives of the tribes of Israel. These men were appointed to oversee the fair distribution of the lands of Canaan after the conquest. It is a prominent role in the organization of the people during their settlement in the promised land.

sens: Man of the united monarchy period in Israel
Son of Laish of Gallim
Husband of Michal, daughter of King Saul
H6409H.detail: Palthiel is a man who lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was unified under one king. He was the son of Laish, a resident of Gallim. King Saul had given him Michal, his own daughter, in marriage. However, Michal had originally been the wife of the prophet David, but after Saul chased and exiled him, the king took Michal back and gave her to Palthiel. Many years later, when David became king and Saul was dead, the military leader Abner demanded the return of Michal to David: it was then that Palthiel, who loved his wife, had to let her go (2 Samuel 3:15).
H6409H.origine: The name Palthiel means "God delivers": it combines two Hebrew words, one meaning "to deliver" and the other "God." It is a theophoric name, that is, it carries the name of God, like many Israelite names. Another similar name, Palti, likely refers to the same person or a variant of the same name.
H6409H.emploi: Palthiel appears only once in the text of the Segond, in 2 Samuel 3:15. He is presented as the one to whom King Saul had given Michal in marriage after having removed David. His role is secondary: it illustrates the consequences of Saul's jealousy towards David, and the suffering that royal politics caused ordinary people. He is a man attached to his wife, as the text mentions that he followed her weeping when she was taken back to be returned to David.
H6409H.portee: The story of Palthiel shows how the decisions of the powerful — Saul's jealousy, political ambitions — fall upon ordinary people and break their lives. It also reminds us of humble faithfulness: Palthiel loved his wife, even though he had to lose her. It is a lesson in compassion for those who suffer from the injustices of power.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H6410G.detail: Pelathia is the name of a man from Judah mentioned only once in the royal genealogies. He is the son of Hanania and the grandson of Zerubbabel, who led the return of the exiles from Babylon (1 Chronicles 3:21). The name recorded in this genealogy testifies to the continuity of David's lineage after the exile.
H6410G.origine: The name Pelathia comes from Hebrew and means "God delivers" or "the Lord delivers." It is composed of elements that express the divine act of liberation, a central idea in the history of Israel, especially during great deliverances (Egypt, Babylonian exile). This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common among the Hebrews to remind of divine protection.
H6410G.emploi: Pelathia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:21, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Zerubbabel. He is listed among the sons of Hanania, alongside his brothers Isaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, and Shecaniah. This very brief mention, without details about his life or role, shows that the Bible simply preserves the memory of his existence in the royal lineage of Judah after the return from exile.

sens: Character of the Old Testament, military leader of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah
H6410H.detail: Pelathia is a man of the tribe of Simeon mentioned only once in the Bible. He lived during the time of King Hezekiah of Judah and led a group of five hundred warriors who fought victoriously against the Amalekites who had taken refuge in the mountain of Seir (1 Chronicles 4:42). His name means "The Lord delivers," reflecting the trust in God in the ancient mentality of Israel.
H6410H.origine: The name Pelathia comes from Hebrew and literally means "The Lord delivers": it associates the divine name with the idea of deliverance. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel and expressed the family's faith in divine protection. Several characters bore this name in the history of Israel.
H6410H.emploi: The Bible mentions at least two or three men bearing the name Pelathia at different times. The one mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:42 was a military leader of Simeon under Hezekiah. Other Pelathia are named in the books of Nehemiah and Ezekiel, including a son of Benaiah and a prince against whom the prophet Ezekiel was commanded to prophesy. The repeated presence of this name suggests that it was honored and borne by important families in Israel.

sens: Leader of the people of Israel who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H6410I.detail: 1. Pelathia is the name of a man who lived during the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He appears in the list of leaders of the people who affixed their seal to the covenant document, committing the people to obey the Law of God (Nehemiah 10:22). He was one of the spiritual and political leaders of Israel during this critical time when the people were recommitting themselves to the Lord.
H6410I.origine: The name Pelathia literally means "Jehovah delivers" in Hebrew: it comes from the root that expresses the idea of deliverance or salvation. This name reflects the faith of the parents in the saving power of God, a central conviction in the life of the Hebrew people.
H6410I.emploi: Pelathia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:22, among the signatories of the solemn covenant that the people returned from exile swore before God. This act of sealing the covenant was essential: it marked the collective commitment of the people to uphold the Law and to turn away from the idolatrous practices that had led to the exile. Pelathia, as a leader, represented a part of the people in this process of spiritual renewal.
H6410I.portee: This moment when Pelathia and his peers seal the covenant reminds believers today of the value of personal and communal renewal before God. The very name, "Jehovah delivers," evokes that only trust in divine deliverance and obedience to His Word can truly free the people from their spiritual chains.

sens: Leader of the people in Judah during the exile
Son of Benaja, prince of Israel
H6410J.detail:
1. Pelathia is a political and military leader who lived in Jerusalem during the return from exile, at the time of the prophet Ezekiel. He is part of the princes and elders who lead the people in the city (Ezekiel 11:1).
2. He is the son of Benaja, a man of authority in the community. His role as leader of the people places him among the most important officials of Jerusalem at that time (Ezekiel 11:1).
H6410J.origine: The name Pelathia means in Hebrew "God delivers" or "the Lord saves." It is composed of two elements: "pelat" (to deliver, to escape) and "Yah" (God). It is a typical theophoric name of ancient Israel, expressing trust in God's saving intervention. Several men have borne this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H6410J.emploi: Pelathia appears twice in the book of Ezekiel, both in chapter 11. He is first presented as one of the twenty-five men that the prophet sees at the eastern gate of the temple, and he is specifically named as a leader of the people alongside Jaazania (Ezekiel 11:1). Shortly thereafter, as Ezekiel prophesies against these leaders who gave bad counsel to the people, Pelathia suddenly dies, which deeply disturbs the prophet and prompts him to intercede for the survivors of Israel (Ezekiel 11:13). This death illustrates God's judgment against the false leaders of the people.
H6410J.portee: The mention of Pelathia teaches that even the apparent leaders of God's people can oppose His will and receive His judgment. His sudden death, occurring at the moment when Ezekiel prophesies his condemnation, shows that human authority cannot prevail against the word of God. It is a reminder for the believer of the importance of listening to true prophets and seeking God's direction rather than following the misleading counsel of religious or political leaders.

sens: Levite priest during the time of Nehemiah
Man who helped Ezra explain the Law to the people
Signatory of the covenant with Nehemiah
H6411A.detail: Pelaja is a Levite (assistant priest) who lived during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem, around the 5th century BCE. In Nehemiah 8:7, he is among the Levites who "explained the law to the people": while Ezra read the book of the Law before the assembled crowd, Pelaja and his companions helped everyone understand what was read, "and each remained in their place." It was a pedagogical and interpretive role during a crucial moment when the people were returning from exile and discovering or rediscovering the Word of God. In Nehemiah 10:10, Pelaja is mentioned again as one of those who sealed the covenant, that is, who solemnly committed, along with Nehemiah, to observe the Law of the Lord and to live according to it. His name means "the Lord does wonders."
H6411A.origine: The Hebrew name Pelaja (פְּלָאיָה) literally means "the Lord (Yah) does wonders (pelé)." It expresses trust in God's miraculous power. This name belongs to the family of theophoric names, that is, names composed with the divine name Yah, common among the Hebrews.
H6411A.emploi: Pelaja is mentioned twice in the book of Nehemiah, both passages relating to the events of the return from exile to Jerusalem. He first appears in Nehemiah 8:7 as one of the Levites responsible for explaining the Law to the people during the great assembly, and then in Nehemiah 10:10 as a signatory of the solemn covenant that the leaders of the people made to commit to observing the Law. These two mentions present him in a role of spiritual guide and religious leader, testifying to the importance of his ministry in the reconstruction of the Jewish community after the exile.
H6411A.portee: Pelaja embodies the role of the Levite in transmitting the Word of God to the people. His ministry reminds us that understanding Scripture is not automatic: it requires faithful teachers who explain and help discern the meaning of divine commandments. His commitment to sealing the covenant also shows how spiritual leaders must be the first to personally commit to obeying the Law, setting an example for the people.

sens: son of Eljoenaï, of the royal lineage of Judah
H6411B.detail: Pelaja is a character from the Old Testament mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of David. He is the son of Eljoenaï and is part of the royal lineage of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 3:24). His name appears in a list of brothers, alongside Hodavia, Eliashib, Akkub, Johanan, Delajah, and Anani.
H6411B.origine: The name Pelaja comes from Hebrew and means "Jehovah does wonders" or "Jehovah is wonderful," composed of an element that evokes the extraordinary works of God. This name reflects the faith of the people of Judah and their desire to recognize divine action in the generations that bear this name.
H6411B.emploi: Pelaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:24, in the genealogy of the sons of Eljoenaï. He is listed among seven brothers recorded in the genealogical register, which shows the continuity of the royal line of David after the Babylonian exile. His appearance in this context indicates that he was an important descendant of the royal house of Judah.

sens: One who flees, who runs away from immediate danger
One who escapes from a catastrophe or judgment
One who escapes from a situation of captivity or domination
H6412A.detail:
1. A fugitive is a person who hastily flees from a place or a dangerous situation. In Genesis 14:13, a fugitive comes to announce to Abram the capture of Lot; he is a messenger who escaped from the battle and runs to tell what he has seen. In Judges 12:5, the fugitives of Ephraim attempt to cross the fords of the Jordan to save themselves after a defeat.
2. The word also refers to one who would survive a judgment or destruction. In Lamentations 2:22, there were "neither fugitive nor survivor" — the term expresses the idea that no one will remain after the calamity. It has a broader meaning: one who escapes death, not necessarily by fleeing.
3. Ezekiel 33:21 shows a man who had "escaped" from besieged Jerusalem and comes to bring the news. He is one who manages to leave a city or a place of captivity despite the circumstances.
H6412A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to escape, to evade." It expresses the idea of a rapid and often perilous flight. This word belongs to a family of terms that speak of evasion and salvation: one who flees seeks to preserve their life by hastily leaving a place. The image is that of urgent and necessary movement to save oneself.
H6412A.emploi: This word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and in historical narratives. It primarily characterizes the fugitives of battle (Genesis 14, Judges 12), then takes on a theological dimension: those who "escape" God's judgment. Ezekiel returns to this theme several times to describe the survivors of the siege of Jerusalem. The word emphasizes less the act of fleeing than the status of one who remains alive after a disaster — a fragile status often accompanied by shame or mourning.
H6412A.portee: The "fugitive" in the Bible is never a glorious character: it is one who survives by chance or divine grace, often alone, bearing bad news or a lesson of judgment. For the reader, this word reminds us that even in catastrophes, some remain alive — either to testify or to be called to repentance. It invites recognition of the fragility of life and the reality of divine judgment, but also the possibility of escape for those who turn to God.

sens: one who has fled from danger
one who has managed to escape death or capture
messenger who brings news of salvation or judgment
H6412B.detail:
1. A fugitive is someone who flees from immediate danger, often a military defeat or a catastrophe. In Numbers 21:29, it refers to the sons of Moab turned into fugitives by defeat, forced to flee to save their lives.
2. More broadly, the word refers to one who has managed to escape death, capture, or judgment — a survivor. Jeremiah 44:14 speaks of the few survivors of Judah who will remain among the exiles in Egypt, and Jeremiah 51:50 calls those who have escaped the sword to leave Babylon.
3. The fugitive can also be a messenger: in Jeremiah 50:28, it is the fugitives who cry out and escape from Babylon to announce the vengeance of the Lord. They bring the news of God's judgment to the survivors left in Zion.
H6412B.origine: This word comes from the Hebrew root "pélat" (פלט), which means "to escape" or "to disengage." It is an action verb: to flee, to save oneself, to escape from peril. The noun "fugitive" (פָּלֵיט) thus designates one who has carried out this action, one who has fled. The family of this word encompasses all meanings related to evasion and survival in the face of danger.
H6412B.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Bible, almost always in the context of catastrophe or judgment. In Numbers and Jeremiah, it describes the survivors of a military defeat or destruction: the fugitives of Moab (Numbers 21:29), the few survivors of Judah scattered in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:14), the fugitives escaping from besieged Babylon (Jeremiah 50:28). In Jeremiah 51:50, the term directly addresses those who have escaped the Babylonian sword. Isaiah 66:19 broadens the meaning: the survivors of divine judgment become messengers sent to announce the glory of the Lord to the nations. The word thus embodies both flight, survival, and the hope of salvation.
H6412B.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God always preserves a remnant — survivors who escape judgment. Those who flee to the Lord, who flee from sin and save themselves in Him, become messengers of His glory. It is a word of hope: even in catastrophes, there are survivors, and God uses them to testify to His power and mercy.

sens: One who escapes from danger, capture, or certain death
The collective of survivors from a catastrophe, war, or punishment
The remnant of the people that God preserves despite judgment
H6413.detail:
1. The survivor is one who flees an immediate danger and manages to get away: in Genesis 32:8, Jacob fears Esau and says that if one of his camps is struck, "the camp that remains may escape," meaning to flee and survive. It is the idea of the fugitive who escapes misfortune.
2. By extension, the word refers to the survivors of a great catastrophe: in 2 Samuel 15:14, David says, "there will be no escape for us before Absalom," meaning there will be no survivors if we stay. The word then encompasses all those who remain alive after a judgment or destruction.
3. In prophetic language especially, the survivor takes on a spiritual meaning: it is the remnant of God's people that the Lord intentionally preserves. In Isaiah 37:32, "from Jerusalem a remnant will go out, and from Mount Zion survivors," which speaks of those whom God keeps to fulfill His promises despite the Assyrian threat.
H6413.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to flee" or "to escape." It first designates the action of fleeing from danger, then the people who flee, and finally the result of that flight: the fact of being saved. The Hebrew word פָּלַט (palaṭ) means "to glide away" or "to escape," from which derives פְּלֵיטָה (peleyṭah), the action noun that designates the escape and the one who escapes.
H6413.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, etc.), in historical books (Samuel, Chronicles), and in the narratives of Ezra-Nehemiah. In its primary sense, it describes the fugitives from a battle or peril (2 Samuel 15:14, Jeremiah 25:35). But from Ezra and particularly in Isaiah, the word changes in scope: it designates the remnant of the people that God has decided to preserve and not destroy. In Isaiah 4:2, the "survivors of Israel" are promised a future blessing: it is the hope of the faithful remnant. The term thus shifts from a human and political sense (survivors of a defeat) to a theological sense (holy remnant preserved by divine mercy).
H6413.portee: This word reminds the believer that God never completely destroys His people. Even in judgment, the Lord preserves a remnant to fulfill His covenant and His promises. It is a source of hope: when the threat seems overwhelming, God always saves a part so that His plan continues. This truth of the "remnant" runs throughout all Scripture and culminates in the promise of salvation in Christ.

sens: One who renders justice, who arbitrates a dispute
One who evaluates, who measures the value or merit of something
One who recognizes or attests something
H6414.detail:
1. The judge is the person invested with the authority to settle a dispute between two parties. In Exodus 21:22, when men quarrel and accidentally injure a pregnant woman, the fine must be "before the judges" — these are the official arbiters who determine the harm and set the compensation. This is the most direct meaning: rendering justice by weighing the facts and deciding.
2. The judge is also one who evaluates or assesses something — its value, quality, or nature. In Deuteronomy 32:31, the expression "Our enemies judge this" means that the enemies themselves can recognize or evaluate it: they are witnesses and attest to the power of the rock of Israel in contrast to their own weakness. This is less about legal judgment and more about discerning and recognizing.
3. By extension, to be a judge of something is to recognize it, to witness it. In Job 31:11, adultery is "a crime that judges punish" — here the judges are those who see, who know, and who punish evil.
H6414.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to divide," "to separate" — the image of the judge who separates the righteous from the guilty, who decides between two opposing positions. The same root gives words for "judgment," "discernment," and even "opinion" (which requires discernment). In the Old Testament, the judge is not only an administrative function but also one that requires moral discernment and wisdom.
H6414.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the provided passages. In Exodus 21:22, it refers to the judge in the institutional and judicial sense: one who sits to apply the law and set fines. In Deuteronomy 32:31, the meaning broadens: the enemy himself is a "judge" of Israel's power — he evaluates its reality. In Job 31:11, the judges are witnesses of divine justice who punish crime. The word thus shifts from the official role of magistrate to the broader role of discerning witness recognizing reality.
H6414.portee: This word reminds us that justice is not merely an administrative function, but is linked to wisdom and discernment. For the Christian, it evokes that God Himself is the ultimate judge of our actions — not a distant or bureaucratic judge, but one who clearly sees the reality of the heart. It is also a call to handle disputes with fair justice and to humbly recognize when one is in the wrong.

sens: Action of rendering a judgment, deciding between two parties
Function, office of a judge
Decision rendered by a judge
Aid, protection provided by a just decision
H6415.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of judging, settling a dispute: it is the function of the judge who listens to both sides and pronounces his decision. In Isaiah 16:3, the fugitive pleads with the king of Moab: "do justice," meaning render me a favorable decision, protect me by your judgment.
2. It is also the charge, the office of the judge himself — the responsibility of one who must judge wisely.
3. By extension, "justice" can refer to the decision itself, the judgment rendered.
4. In a context of protest or distress, the word takes on a nuance of recourse: to ask for justice is to ask to be defended, to be protected by a favorable judgment.
H6415.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to separate," "to distinguish," "to judge." It is related to the role of the judge who must separate good from evil, the guilty from the innocent. It is in the same realm as the word "judge" itself. The word expresses the idea that rendering justice is primarily about establishing a clear distinction, a sharp boundary between two opposing positions.
H6415.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 16:3). Moab, threatened by invasion, cries out to the king to render justice — that is, to make a protective decision. The context shows that "doing justice" here means granting asylum and protection to the one who pleads. The word remains infrequent, but its meaning remains constant: the judge's responsibility to decide and protect.
H6415.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God is the supreme Judge who renders justice equitably. It also shows that justice is not abstract: it is a concrete act of protecting the weak. To ask for justice is to appeal to the wisdom and strength of the one who can defend us — an attitude of trust in God and His representatives.

sens: one who renders justice, who judges cases
pertaining to justice, judgment
guilty, subject to judgment
H6416.detail:
1. The judge is one who renders justice and pronounces judgments. In Job 31:28, Job asserts that if he had worshiped idols, it would be a crime that the judges should punish: idolatry is a serious offense that falls under judicial authority.
2. The adjective also describes what pertains to the domain of law and judgment. It is a judicial matter, a case that calls for a judgment, a sentence.
3. By extension, it can designate a person who is subject to judgment, guilty, liable to condemnation: someone who deserves to be brought before justice.
H6416.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root פלל (palal), which means "to judge" or "to decide." This root evokes the idea of deciding between two things, separating the just from the unjust. The adjective פְּלִילִי expresses what directly concerns this function of judgment and condemnation.
H6416.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 31:28, in the context where Job enumerates the sins he has not committed. There he designates the "judges" who should have punished idolatry as a serious crime. The context shows that Job respects the moral and divine order embodied by the justice of earthly judges. This passage reveals the biblical conception of the judiciary as a reflection of divine justice.
H6416.portee: This word reminds us that justice is not an arbitrary human creation, but a reflection of God's justice. For Job, respecting judges and their verdicts is to honor the moral order that God has established. It invites the reader to see in judicial institutions an expression of divine governance over the world.

sens: The rendering of a decision, the judgment rendered by one who has authority
The exercise of discernment and reasoning to decide equitably
The impartial administration of the law
H6417.detail: 1. The word concretely denotes the act of rendering a judgment, giving a decision: this is what a judge or a prophet does when he must settle a question. In Isaiah 28:7, the prophets and priests who stagger in drunkenness can no longer render "justice" — they lose the ability to judge rightly. 2. The term emphasizes the reasoning, the reflection necessary to arrive at a just conclusion: to judge is not to guess, it is to weigh the arguments. 3. It is also the administration of the law in the community, the work of one who has the duty to govern equitably and maintain order according to God's law.
H6417.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to judge," "to decide" (related to other biblical words for judgment and judicial authority). Its initial image is the act of separating, distinguishing the good from the bad, the guilty from the innocent. In biblical Hebrew, this root carries the idea of moral discernment and authoritative decision.
H6417.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in this sense: Isaiah 28:7. The context is a severe critique of the religious authorities of Israel — prophets and priests — who become intoxicated. By staggering in wine, they lose the clear judgment that is essential to their office: rendering "justice" rightly, that is, interpreting God's Word and applying the law with clarity of mind. The prophet Isaiah stigmatizes here not only drunkenness but the corruption of spiritual and judicial discernment.
H6417.portee: This word reminds us that judgment, just discernment, is a gift that requires mental and moral clarity. Spiritual leaders — like every Christian called to discern — need a clear mind, freed from the passions that disturb the heart. It is an invitation to take seriously the sobriety of life and thought that the exercise of responsibility before God demands.

sens: Administrative or territorial zone of a city or region
Part of territory entrusted to a responsible chief
Spindle or stick used in the work of spinning thread
H6418.detail:
1. In the context of Nehemiah, a "district" is an administrative area of Jerusalem or its surroundings, placed under the responsibility of a local chief. When the text states that Rephaiah is "chief of half the district of Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 3:9), it refers to a portion of the urban territory that this leader was overseeing for the reconstruction of the walls. It is a practical territorial division for organizing work and administration.
2. The word can also more broadly refer to a circuit or constituency: a defined area that one traverses or administers. Malchijah is "chief of the district of Beth-Hakkarem" (Nehemiah 3:14), a region with its own borders and management.
3. In a concrete and ancient sense, it primarily refers to the spindle or stick on which thread is wound. The passage in Proverbs 31:19 (“She puts her hand to the spindle”) evokes this image of the stick that turns to wind the fiber and create the thread — hence the idea of a circular area or a division that “turns around” a central point.
H6418.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the movement of rotation and division. The spindle, a rotating stick used in spinning thread, suggests the idea of a circle or circuit; thus, a "district" is named for a defined area, a territory that “turns” around an administrative center, just as the spindle divides and organizes the thread.
H6418.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the book of Nehemiah (six occurrences), during the account of the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the exile. Each time, it designates a portion of the city or its region for which a chief was responsible: "chief of the district of Mizpah," "chief of the district of Beth-Tsur," etc. This administrative and local usage anchors the word in a concrete reality: organizing work by dividing the territory. One occurrence in 2 Samuel 3:29 uses the form "stick" (spindle) in the literal sense, while Proverbs 31:19 also retains it literally. The word never strays from these practical and earthly contexts.
H6418.portee: For the Christian reading Nehemiah, this word reminds us that the reconstruction of Israel after the exile was accomplished through local and responsible organization: each district chief had a specific charge, a section of the wall to repair. It illustrates how God restores His people through organized work and shared responsibilities — each having their clearly defined task. It is a sober lesson on order and cooperation in the common work.

sens: To address a request, a supplication to God
To intercede with someone on behalf of a third party
To implore, to plead insistently
H6419.detail:
1. To pray is to speak to God to present a request, a prayer, or a supplication. This is the most common form of the word: someone turns to God to tell Him what they desire or need. Samuel says to Israel: "I will pray to the Lord for you" (1 Samuel 7:5), meaning he will make a request to God on behalf of His people.
2. The word can also mean to intercede, that is, to intervene with someone on behalf of another. Abimelech asks Abraham: "You will pray for me" (Genesis 20:7), which means: you will ask God to show me His favor. It is an act of mediation between God and a man.
3. Finally, to pray expresses the idea of pleading with urgency and humility. In Isaiah 45:14, the peoples bow down and speak "pleadingly": this is to pray with the intensity and sincerity of someone who knows they are entirely dependent on the one to whom they are addressing.
H6419.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of intervening, of placing oneself between two parties. The word is used in the intensified form (Piel) to express the action of mediating or judging, and in the reflexive form (Hithpael) for personal intercession and prayer. Prayer is thus conceived as an action where the one who prays stands before God, often for another, taking on the role of intercessor.
H6419.emploi: This verb appears 82 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Daniel). It describes decisive moments when a man of God intercedes for his people or for a dangerous situation. Samuel prays for Israel (1 Samuel 7:5), Hezekiah prays when he is ill (2 Kings 20:2), Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven (Nehemiah 2:4). The word is also frequent in the Psalms, where it expresses the personal prayer of the faithful. Prayer can be silent (1 Samuel 1:12) or expressed in words, in the temple or anywhere else. It often accompanies the confession of sins and the expectation of divine intervention.
H6419.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that prayer is not an isolated practice, but a living action where the believer stands before God, either for themselves or to intercede on behalf of others. It shows that in the Bible, prayer is a form of intimacy with God, where one can present everything to Him. It is also an act of faith: the one who prays acknowledges that only God can intervene and transform situations.

sens: Jewish man from the time of the return from exile
son of Uzzai
worker who contributed to the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem
H6420.detail: Palal is a Jew who participated in the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah, during the return from Babylonian exile. He was the son of Uzzai and worked on the section of the corner of the wall and the upper tower of the king's palace (Nehemiah 3:25). Although mentioned only once in the Bible, his name and that of his fellow workers testify to the collective mobilization to rebuild the city.
H6420.origine: The name Palal literally means "judge" in Hebrew, coming from the root that expresses the idea of judging or discerning. This name reflects the importance given to justice and authority in Israelite society, even though it is borne here by a simple worker in the reconstruction project.
H6420.emploi: Palal is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:25. He appears in the list of those who participated in the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile around 445 BC. This passage systematically enumerates the builders and the sections of the wall for which they were responsible, and Palal occupies a place marking his role in this great restoration effort of the city.
H6420.portee: The mention of Palal and his fellow workers reminds us that the great projects of God are not accomplished by a few great names, but by the faithful mobilization of many ordinary people. The return from exile and the reconstruction of Jerusalem are major acts of the divine plan, made possible by the humble contribution of each individual.

sens: Man living during the time of Exile and Return
H6421.detail: Pélalia is an ancestor of the priest Adajah mentioned in the genealogical list of priests who returned to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (Nehemiah 11:12). He was the father of Jerocham and the son of Amzi.
H6421.origine: The name Pélalia means "the Lord has judged" in Hebrew. It is composed of the element "pel" (judgment) and the divine name "Yah." This name expresses trust in divine justice, a particular appropriateness for a priestly family.
H6421.emploi: Pélalia appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:12, in a genealogy of the priests established after the return from exile. He is presented as the father of Jerocham and the grandfather of Adajah, a priest who lived in Jerusalem. This mention shows that his descendants held an important place among the clergy of restored Jerusalem.

sens: an indeterminate person, someone undefined
an unnamed but present interlocutor
H6422.detail:
1. The word designates a person whose name is unknown or whose identity is not specified — simply "someone," "a certain person." It's like saying "so-and-so" in English when you don't know the name or prefer not to give it. In Daniel 8:13, the angel speaking to Moses (or rather in the vision, the first saint) refers to "this one" — another saint — and it is a polite way to refer to his unnamed interlocutor without specifying or describing who he is exactly.
2. In the dynamics of the text, this word creates a certain distance: it designates someone who is there, who is listening, but remains deliberately vague, even mysterious. It's the equivalent of "you who are listening" or "that other character" when one wants to maintain a certain abstraction rather than naming.
H6422.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of indeterminacy, of someone whose identity is not specified. There is another, more common form (פְּלֹנִי, Peloni), which has exactly the same meaning. It is a rare word, used to refer to a character in a deliberately imprecise or anonymous manner.
H6422.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 8:13. It occurs in a vision where two saints are dialoguing: one speaks of the vision of the perpetual sacrifice and the desolation of the sanctuary, and the text reports that another saint (designated by this indefinite word) asks how long this situation will last. Its unique use underscores the mysterious and celestial atmosphere of the vision, where the characters remain spiritual entities without precise identification.
H6422.portee: This word reminds us that in visions and divine mysteries, the precise identity of angels or celestial beings matters less than their role and message. It invites the reader to focus on what is being said and what is happening, rather than on human details. It is an invitation to humility in the face of the invisible world: some things remain veiled, and this is not a weakness of the text, but a wisdom.

sens: an indeterminate person, whose name one does not want or cannot give
H6423.detail: 1. This word designates a person whose identity remains vague or deliberately hidden. It is used when speaking of someone without naming them: it is like saying "a certain" or "such a person." In Ruth 4:1, Boaz speaks to "such and such" (the one who has the right of redemption) without naming him at first; it is a way to maintain suspense. 2. The word is also used for someone that cannot be clearly identified: in 1 Samuel 21:2, David speaks of "such a man" to whom he would have given an appointment, speaking vaguely. 3. It can also express anonymity or indifference regarding identity: in 2 Kings 6:8, it is said that such a place was a passageway, without needing to specify further.
H6423.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "this one" or "this place," with a nuance of indeterminacy. The form peloni is constructed to remain vague and anonymous, unlike proper names that identify precisely. It is a linguistic tool for speaking about something or someone without naming them.
H6423.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Ruth 4:1, it designates the anonymous kinsman-redeemer until Boaz names him. In 1 Samuel 21:2, it is an example where David uses vagueness to invent an excuse to the priest. In 2 Kings 6:8, it refers to an anonymous place on the way to Israel. Each time, the intention is to speak of someone or something without revealing or knowing the precise identity.
H6423.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible names and highlights those it deems important for the story of salvation, while the anonymous remain in the shadows. It is also a literary device that creates suspense: in Ruth, the "such and such" soon becomes a name and a story. This shows how important naming is in the biblical project.

sens: Weigh something on a scale, determine its weight
Balance, make equal or smooth
Examine carefully, consider attentively
Let something unfold freely, allow it to develop
Direct, arrange, regulate a path or conduct
H6424.detail:
1. Weigh on a scale: the primary, concrete meaning. The one who weighs places an object on a plate and observes the balance. In Psalms 58:3, the wicked "weigh" (place) the violence of their hands on the scale, a striking image of the deliberate calculation of evil.

2. Make smooth, even, equal: a rough path becomes flat and passable when it is leveled. This is why the righteous "levels" the path of the righteous in Isaiah 26:7: he makes the way of justice straight and easy.

3. Examine carefully, weigh in one's mind: when one "considers" the path one takes (Proverbs 4:26), one examines it, weighs it mentally before proceeding. The Lord "observes" all the paths of man (Proverbs 5:21) by scrutinizing them carefully.

4. Let go freely, give free rein: in Psalms 78:50, God gave "free" course to His anger, meaning He unleashed it, allowed it to act without restraint.
H6424.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of weighing and balancing. This image of weight and scale gradually enriches: weighing objects means examining them; weighing a path mentally means considering it; weighing a will means allowing it to express itself freely. The word belongs to the family of terms of measurement and balance, which are very important in biblical wisdom.
H6424.emploi: This verb appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs) and the Psalms. In the Psalms, it describes the divine action of observing and scrutinizing (Psalms 5:21), or the human action of weighing evil (Psalms 58:3). In Proverbs, it teaches the youth to "consider" their steps (Proverbs 4:26) and warns against the adulterous woman who "does not consider" the path of life (Proverbs 5:6). In Isaiah 26:7, it describes the righteous who "levels" the path. The meaning varies according to the context: careful examination, balancing, free unfolding, or smoothing of a path.
H6424.portee: This word teaches the believer that his steps, his paths, and his choices are under the watchful eye of God who "observes" them. It also calls him to "consider" his ways before acting, to weigh his decisions in his heart. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance: to examine one's path so that it remains straight, like the righteous who levels his path. Evil, on the other hand, unfolds when one ceases to weigh one's actions.

sens: scale or instrument for weighing and comparing weights
hook or rod used to suspend and balance what is weighed
action of weighing, measuring fairly
just measure and judgment of God
H6425.detail:
1. The balance is the basic instrument of commerce and measurement: two pans in equilibrium on a beam, where goods are placed on one side and weights on the other to determine the exact weight (Proverbs 16:11).
2. The word also refers to the hook or metal rod that supports and balances the pans, allowing for precise comparison (Isaiah 40:12: "weighed the mountains with a hook").
3. The balance symbolizes fairness and justice in transactions: having just balances means rejecting fraud and commercial deceit (Proverbs 16:11: "All the weights of the bag are His work").
4. Figuratively, the balance becomes the image of divine judgment: God alone holds the true measure and weight of all things, including the hearts and actions of humans.
H6425.origine: The Hebrew word péles comes from the root that evokes the action of weighing and suspending. It belongs to the family of terms related to balance and measurement. The image is very concrete: it is the object seen every day at the market or with the merchant, the one that gives everyone confidence (or distrust) in commerce.
H6425.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Proverbs 16:11, it refers to the just balance, an instrument of commercial integrity and a reflection of God's character: "The just weight and balance are the Lord's." In Isaiah 40:12, in a context of divine greatness, the prophet describes God weighing the mountains and hills "with a hook" and on the balance, measuring the entire universe with absolute precision. In both cases, the balance is associated with justice, fairness, and God's sovereignty over all things.
H6425.portee: For the believer, the balance reminds us that God is perfectly just and knows the true weight of all things — our hearts, our words, our actions. It invites integrity in business and daily life, rejecting fraud and deceit. It also assures that nothing escapes divine justice: God measures everything with a fairness that no earthly commerce can match.

sens: To tremble or sway under a shock, a jolt
To be shaken physically in stability
To lose footing or assurance under a force
H6426.detail: 1. The verb literally describes the action of trembling or moving violently under an impact: in Job 9:6, the pillars of the earth are "shaken" when God shakes the earth from its base, as if a powerful force makes them sway and tremble. It is the physical image of a structure temporarily losing its solidity. 2. Figuratively, the word evokes the idea of being destabilized, shaken internally — not only in the body but in confidence or assurance. However, with only one biblical usage, the primary meaning predominates: the physical movement of something that is shaken.
H6426.origine: The verb הִתְפָּלַץ (hithpael from the root פלץ) expresses trembling or shaking. The root suggests a violent movement, an agitation. In biblical Hebrew, verbs in the hithpael (reflexive form) often indicate an action experienced or a state entered into — here, being shaken, being in tremor. Words from this family all refer to sudden movement and imbalance.
H6426.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 9:6. In this grand passage, Job contemplates divine omnipotence: God shakes the earth from its base, and the pillars that support it are shaken, meaning they are shaken, swaying. Job uses this cosmic image to express the immensity of divine force against which everything that seems stable and unchanging can tremble. The context is one of meditation on God's irresistible power.
H6426.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the solidity of the world, even that of the foundations of the earth, is nothing compared to the power of God. For a believer in distress or doubt, this can evoke both the fragility of human certainties and the greatness of the one who holds everything in His hands — an invitation to place trust, not in what can be shaken, but in God alone.

sens: Involuntary shivering of the body seized by fear
Paralytic dread
Feeling of terror that grips someone
H6427.detail:
1. Trembling is primarily a physical reaction: the body shivers, shaken by intense fear. Job describes this experience by saying "a trembling grips my body" (Job 21:6), as if terror were a force that invades him inescapably.
2. The word also denotes the dread itself, this feeling of horror that paralyzes. In Psalm 55, the psalmist speaks of "fear and trembling" that assail him (Psalms 55:6), a fear so strong that it overwhelms him like a wave.
3. Trembling can also evoke the enveloping atmosphere of terror that covers a person or a moment. When Ezekiel describes divine judgment, he says that "terror envelops them" (Ezekiel 7:18), as if fear were a garment that completely covers them.
H6427.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of curling up, folding in on oneself out of fear. The image is that of a person seized by such sudden and intense fright that they lose control of themselves, both physically and morally. It is an instinctive reaction to danger or horror.
H6427.emploi: This word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the poetic and prophetic books: Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. It always describes an intense and personal experience of fear: Job speaking of divine judgment (Job 21:6), the psalmist facing his enemies (Psalms 55:6), Isaiah troubled by a vision (Isaiah 21:4), Ezekiel describing the day of judgment on Israel (Ezekiel 7:18). In each case, trembling is a reaction to something terrible or supernatural.
H6427.portee: This word reminds us that fear is a legitimate reaction to horror or divine judgment, and it can seize even the righteous. It is not a weakness, but a natural human reaction to what exceeds our understanding or to danger. However, it also invites us to seek trust in God rather than remain paralyzed by it.

sens: To roll, to wallow in the ashes or dust
Gesture of mourning, lamentation, and deep desolation
Expression of intense affliction in the face of calamity
H6428.detail:
1. The word literally describes the action of rolling on the ground, wallowing in ashes or dust. It is a concrete physical gesture, often public: in Jeremiah 6:26, the daughter of Judah is called to "roll in the ashes" as a sign of mourning in the face of the coming devastator.
2. This gesture expresses deep mourning and ritual lamentation. In biblical times, rolling in ashes was a way to show one's affliction, humiliation, and sorrow in the face of a loss or disaster. This is why the shepherds in Jeremiah 25:34 are called to roll in the ashes upon learning that they will be slaughtered.
3. The meaning extends to the expression of total desolation in the face of public and collective misfortunes. In Ezekiel 27:30, the sailors and navigators roll in the ashes upon seeing the destruction of Tyre, embodying the grief of an entire people.
H6428.origine: The verb פָּלַשׁ (palash) comes from a root that evokes the movement of rolling, wallowing in a substance (ashes, dust). In Hebrew, this gesture is part of the rites of mourning and repentance attested in several passages of the Old Testament. The word expresses the idea of voluntarily humiliating oneself by covering oneself with ashes, a symbol of death and nothingness.
H6428.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah and Ezekiel). Each time, it describes the gesture of the inhabitants or leaders who roll in the ashes in reaction to an imminent calamity or destruction. In Jeremiah 6:26 and 25:34, the gesture accompanies mourning and lamentation; in Ezekiel 27:30, it expresses the collective grief of the sailors in the face of the ruin of Tyre. The context is always that of a major tragedy or catastrophe striking Israel or an allied people. It is a rite of deep lamentation, codified in the customs of the ancient Near East.
H6428.portee: For the Christian reader, this gesture reveals the depth of mourning and repentance in the Bible. It shows that the prophets expected the people to have a bodily, visible, and humiliating reaction to God's judgment. It is a reminder that sincere mourning involves the whole person, body and soul, and that true lamentation before God cannot be purely internal. This gesture also illustrates how God takes contrition seriously and how His people were called to visibly manifest their repentance.

sens: people of the western coast of Canaan
territory occupied by this people
set of Philistine lands
H6429.detail:
1. The Philistines are a people who settled on the western coast of Canaan, particularly in the region we now call the coastal Palestine. They posed a significant military threat to Israel, as shown in Exodus 15:14 where "the peoples hear it and tremble" upon hearing about the Philistines.
2. The word also refers to the territory they inhabited, the southwestern coastal region of Canaan, sometimes called "the land of the Philistines." The poetic texts of the Psalms speak of this territory as a power to be feared, capable of "shouting for joy" against enemies (Psalms 108:10).
3. In a broader sense, the term can refer to the entire Philistine world in its relations with Israel and other neighboring peoples, as shown in the list of coalesced enemies in Psalms 83:8: "Gebel, Ammon, Amalek, The Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre."
H6429.origine: The word literally means "land of wanderers" or "land of sojourners," as the Philistines were not originally from Canaan but came from the Aegean region. They gradually settled on the Palestinian coast and founded a distinct people. The Hebrew word פְּלִשְׁתִּי (pelishti, "Philistine") refers to the people themselves, while פְּלֶשֶׁת (Philistia) refers to their territory.
H6429.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and among the prophets. It always refers to the people or territory of the Philistines in the context of their relations with Israel and neighboring nations. In Exodus 15:14, the Philistines embody fear in the face of God's power manifested for Israel. In the Psalms, the "land of the Philistines" is mentioned among the enemies of Israel and surrounding peoples (Psalms 60:10, 108:10), sometimes alongside the Ammonites, Tyrians, or other adversaries. In the prophet Isaiah, the Philistines are political and military rivals to be watched, especially in the context of prophetic threats (Isaiah 14:29). The word always carries a geopolitical dimension: it refers to a foreign power in the ancient Near Eastern world.
H6429.portee: Understanding who the Philistines are helps grasp a constant tension in the biblical narrative: Israel does not live alone in Canaan, but shares this territory with other powerful peoples. The Philistines remind the reader that God's promise to Israel was not automatically fulfilled, but required trust and courage in a hostile environment. The stories of David fighting Goliath or judges confronting the Philistines illustrate this spiritual reality: victory comes from God, not from human strength alone.

sens: Inhabitant of Philistia, coastal region of Canaan
Warlike people who opposed Israel during the judges and royal period
Enemy of Israel, military and cultural rival
H6430G.detail:
1. The Philistines are a people established on the western coast of Canaan, particularly around cities like Gath, Ekron, and Gaza. They come from immigrants from the island of Crete (or Mediterranean regions) who settled in this coastal area. As early as Genesis, we encounter them: Abraham makes a covenant with Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Beer-Sheba (Genesis 21:32).
2. The Philistines are the quintessential enemy people during the time of the Judges. They oppress Israel repeatedly: "The Philistines oppressed the children of Israel" (Judges 10:7). Samson leads a long struggle against them, engaging in singular battles and ambushes that mark his time. At his death, he defeats them again, exclaiming, "Let me die with the Philistines!" (Judges 16:30).
3. Under the reign of Saul and David, the Philistines remain a major military threat. They possess superior weapons: "No blacksmith could be found in all the land of Israel" because the Philistines had confiscated the iron (1 Samuel 13:19). It is against them that David fights the giant Goliath, a battle that symbolizes the confrontation between two peoples and two gods.
H6430G.origine: The Hebrew word literally means "immigrants" or "invaders," reflecting their history: peoples from the Mediterranean who gradually settled on the Palestinian coast. The term also appears in the form "Philistia" (פְּלֶ֫שֶׁת), which designates the region itself. Historically, the Philistines are known in Egyptian sources as the "Sea Peoples" who attempted to invade Egypt in the 12th century BCE.
H6430G.emploi: The word "Philistine" appears 276 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books: Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles. The Philistines first appear sporadically (Genesis), then become a major regional power during the Judges. The conflict intensifies with Samson (Judges 13-16), who individually fights the Philistines for twenty years. In 1 Samuel, they threaten the ark of the covenant (1 Samuel 4-6) and dominate the land until David's victory. The word always designates an inhabitant of a region and a political and military adversary.
H6430G.portee: The Philistines embody in the Bible the organized opposition to God and His people. Their story teaches that faith in God prevails over military strength: Samson defeats a thousand men with a donkey's jawbone, David brings down the giant Goliath with a sling and a stone. The battle against the Philistines shows that God grants victory not to the best armed, but to those who trust Him. It is a lesson of trust for the believer in the face of obstacles.

sens: inhabitant de la Philistie, peuple établi sur la côte occidentale de Canaan
H6430H.detail: The word refers to a Philistine, a member of the people who settled on the coasts of Canaan. According to the Bible, the Philistines descended from Mizraim and came from Caphtor (probably Crete). They first appear in the genealogy of nations after the Flood (Genesis 10:14): "the Casluhim, from whom the Philistines came." This same people will play a major role in the history of Israel, particularly during the time of Samson and King David.
H6430H.origine: The name "Philistine" comes from the Hebrew Pelishti, which literally means "immigrants" or "invaders." It reflects the foreign origin of this people: the Philistines were not native to Canaan but came from elsewhere to settle there. The word also appears in the form "Philistia" to designate their territory.
H6430H.emploi: The word "Philistine" appears twice in the Hebrew Bible in the parallel passages of Genesis 10:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:12, both in the genealogical context of the peoples descended from Noah after the Flood. In these two verses, it is mentioned that the Philistines are descended from the Casluhim. This is a brief mention of their origin. The people of the Philistines become much more present and active in the subsequent narratives, particularly from the Book of Judges.
H6430H.portee: This genealogical mention reminds us that the Philistines, although enemies of the people of God, have a place in God's created order and an origin assigned by the Creator. It invites us to see that all peoples, even those who will resist God's work, belong to the history that God governs.

sens: habitant de Philistie, peuple de la côte ouest de Canaan
guerrier ou adversaire du peuple d'Israël
H6430I.detail:
1. A Philistine is an inhabitant of Philistia, a coastal region to the west of Canaan. This people descends from Mizraim and settled on the lands that God had promised to Israel. In Exodus 23:31, God promises Moses to establish the borders of Israel "to the sea of the Philistines," thus designating the Mediterranean coast as the western boundary of the territory.
2. In biblical history, the Philistines are often the adversaries of Israel — a warrior and powerful people with whom the Israelites have long competed for control of the promised land. This is why the name "Philistine" evokes the opposition and tension between two peoples seeking to dominate the same territory.
H6430I.origine: The Hebrew word פְּלִשְׁתִּי (Philistine) designates a people whose name means "immigrants" or "those from elsewhere." According to the Bible, the Philistines would come from Caphtor, probably Crete. They form a distinct group from the populations of Canaan, identifiable by their foreign origin and coastal settlement. The term "sea of the Philistines" is another way of referring to the Mediterranean, the Great Sea.
H6430I.emploi: The word "Philistine" appears once in this passage from Exodus 23:31, where God delineates the territory He promises to Israel. Here, "the sea of the Philistines" is not primarily a moral judgment on the people themselves, but a geographical indication: it is the western coast of Canaan, the Mediterranean shoreline. This same coastline will indeed be occupied by the Philistines in the historical narratives that follow, particularly during the time of the judges and the early kings of Israel.
H6430I.portee: This passage reminds the believer that God had established a precise plan for Israel: a defined territory with clear boundaries, from the Nile to the Mediterranean. The Philistines then represent a challenge to this divine promise — not because they are intrinsically evil, but because they occupy land promised to Israel. For the Christian reader, this illustrates how God leads His people toward the fulfillment of His promises, even in the face of visible obstacles.

sens: Homme de la tribu de Ruben au temps de l'Exode
Père du rebelle On
H6431G.detail:
1. Peleth is a Reubenite, a member of the tribe of Reuben, who lived during the years in the desert after the exodus from Egypt. His name means "speed" or "flight" in Hebrew, evoking swiftness. He appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 16:1, where he is mentioned as the father of On.
2. On, son of Peleth, is known for his rebellion alongside Dathan and Abiram against Moses and Aaron. Although Peleth himself is not described as participating in this rebellion, his name is linked to this major event of the Exodus through his son.
H6431G.origine: The name Peleth (פלת) derives from a Hebrew root evoking flight or speed. What is remarkable is that although his name suggests swiftness or escape, Peleth remains a discreet figure in biblical history, simply a father mentioned in passing.
H6431G.emploi: Peleth appears only once in Scripture, in Numbers 16:1. He is cited solely for his genealogical link: he is the father of On, who joined Dathan and Abiram in the famous rebellion against the authority of Moses during the forty years of wandering in the desert. This rebellion was dramatically halted when the ground opened up under the rebels. Peleth himself disappears from history after this mention.
H6431G.portee: Peleth reminds us that even marginal names in the Bible have a place in God's narrative. His son was involved in one of the most serious rebellions against the authority that God had established, and the silence about Peleth after this mention may invite the reader to reflect on the consequences of familial disobedience.

sens: fils de Jonathan et descendant de Jérahmeël de Juda
H6431H.detail: Peleth is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible as the son of Jonathan and brother of Zaza. He belongs to the lineage of Jérahmeël, an important family of Judah. He is a link in the genealogy of this tribe, listed during the registration of the families of the chosen people.
H6431H.origine: The name Peleth means "speed" or "swiftness" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of speed or flight. It is a typical theophoric name of the time, perhaps chosen to express a wish for blessing upon the child.
H6431H.emploi: Peleth appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:33, in a genealogical list where the author enumerates the descendants of Jérahmeël. He is presented as the son of Jonathan and the brother of Zaza. These genealogical lists in the Book of Chronicles are historical records of the descendants of the tribes of Israel, preserving the memory of families through the generations.

sens: Close guard of King David
Soldiers who ensure the king's security and service
Probably mercenaries or warriors of foreign origin
H6432.detail:
