1. The Pelethites form a body of guards for King David, alongside the Cherethites: they are elite soldiers, always mentioned together, tasked with the personal protection of the king and the execution of his orders (2 Samuel 8:18, 20:23).
2. They accompany the king on important journeys, such as during the flight from Absalom or the coronation of Solomon, demonstrating their role as an honor guard and trusted armed force (2 Samuel 15:18; 1 Kings 1:38, 1:44).
3. Their exact origin remains obscure, but their constant association with the Cherethites suggests that they may have been mercenaries or warriors recruited from neighboring peoples, a common practice among kings of the ancient Near East.
H6432.origine: The name Pelethites designates the descendants of a person or group called Pelath, whose precise identity eludes us. They are always mentioned in tandem with the Cherethites (whose name may evoke the Cretans), suggesting that these two bodies of guards come from distinct origins. The constant parallelism between these two groups in the Bible indicates that they formed a single military institution.
H6432.emploi: The Pelethites appear seven times in the Bible, all occurrences found in the books of Samuel and Kings. They are always associated with the Cherethites and placed under the command of Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, the most famous of David's officers. They are first seen as palace guards (2 Samuel 8:18, 20:23), then active in critical moments of royal history: during Absalom's rebellion, where they remain loyal to the fleeing king (2 Samuel 15:18), during the pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri (2 Samuel 20:7), and especially during Solomon's coronation, where they play a decisive role in establishing David's chosen successor (1 Kings 1:38, 1:44). Their presence marks the decisive moments of royal power.
H6432.portee: The Pelethites remind us that all human power, even a king anointed by God like David, needs protection and support. They also illustrate how service to the king, even performed by foreigners or mercenaries, is part of the order that God establishes. Their loyalty during crises shows the importance of fidelity in human relationships.

sens: Opening of the head through which one speaks and eats
Mouth of an animal, jaw with teeth
Opening or mouth of an object
H6433.detail:
1. The mouth is the opening of the body through which one utters words and takes in food. When King Nebuchadnezzar receives God's command, "the word was still in the mouth of the king" (Daniel 4:31): the words he spoke were still coming out of his mouth. This is the primary and most common meaning of the word.
2. The mouth of an animal, with its jaws and teeth, ready to bite or devour. Daniel sees in a vision "a horn that had eyes, a mouth speaking arrogantly" (Daniel 7:8), where the mouth represents the ability to dominate and speak as a master. The bear in the vision has "three ribs in its mouth between its teeth" (Daniel 7:5), an image of its devastating power. God "shut the mouths of the lions" (Daniel 6:22) to protect Daniel, showing that even fierce beasts obey God.
3. The opening or entrance of a construction: "they put it over the mouth of the pit" (Daniel 6:17) refers to the opening through which one descends into the pit where the lions were thrown.
H6433.origine: The Aramaic word pum comes from a root that means "mouth" and is related to the Hebrew word peh (פֶּה) with the same meaning. This root relies on a simple and direct image: the visible opening of the face. In Aramaic, as in Hebrew, the mouth is both the seat of speech and the place of taste and flavor.
H6433.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the book of Daniel, regularly designating human mouths that speak (the mouth of King Nebuchadnezzar, that of the horn speaking arrogantly in 7:8 and 7:20) or the mouths of animals endowed with destructive force (the mouths of lions, of the bear). The context of the apocalyptic visions shows that the mouth, in beasts, symbolizes a dominating power, while in humans it marks the power of speech and authority.
H6433.portee: This word reminds us that the mouth is both a source of life (through speech and food) and an instrument of power. In Daniel's visions, seeing a "mouth that speaks arrogantly" invites the reader to meditate on the danger of pride and blasphemy. Understanding that God shuts the "mouths of lions" reinforces the conviction that the Lord commands all of creation, even the fiercest creatures, to protect His children.

sens: The corner of a square or rectangular object, the point where two sides meet
Figuratively, the position of authority or power of a leader or king
H6434.detail:
1. The corner is the point formed by the meeting of two surfaces or two lines. In Zechariah 14:10, the "corner gate" likely refers to a gate of Jerusalem located at an important angle of the city, a notable point of its fortifications.
2. Figuratively, the corner symbolizes a position of strength or authority: a leader is said to be "a corner" to express that he is a pillar, a figure of power. It is the image of the corner that supports and holds everything else up.
H6434.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that designates the corner or angle of a construction. It belongs to the family of words that describe the shape and structure of buildings and cities. The primary image is very concrete: it is the intersection point where walls meet and reinforce each other.
H6434.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in Zechariah 14:10, where it describes one of the gates of Jerusalem. The French translation renders the word as "corners," showing that it refers to a specific and remarkable geographical point in the configuration of the holy city. The context of this passage is the prophetic description of the transformation of Jerusalem at the end of times.
H6434.portee: This corner of Jerusalem reminds us that the holy city has a structure, boundaries, and strong points. In Zechariah's vision, the corner gate is part of the renovated landscape of the coming Kingdom, where every detail—including these corners—holds divine and prophetic significance.

sens: Fear of a dreaded consequence, expressed by one who wants to avoid it
Warning or caution against a possible danger
Negative condition introduced by a hypothesis
Adverbial use marking negation or restriction
H6435.detail:
1. It is the expression of fear in the face of a risk or catastrophe that one wants to prevent. In Genesis 3:3, God says: "You shall not eat of it... lest you die" — the phrase "fear that" expresses the fear that an action may lead to death. It is apprehension: one dreads an outcome and seeks to avert it through prohibition.
2. The word serves to warn someone of danger: it is a caution to prevent them from doing what could lead to their downfall. In Deuteronomy 4:9, "Take heed lest you forget" invites vigilance. Here, the speaker protects the listener by presenting the risk.
3. Sometimes, "fear that" introduces a simple negative condition, without emphasizing emotional fear: in Judges 14:15, "otherwise we will burn you" presents a threatening alternative. The meaning is close to a hypothetical clause: "if you do not do this, then..."
4. In certain contexts, especially with verbs of command or advice, the word functions as a particle of negation or restriction, reinforcing a prohibition or an order.
H6435.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּן (pen) comes from a root expressing the idea of "turning" or "turning away" — the basic image is that of fear that turns us away from danger. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "face" or "direction." It is a very ancient word, fundamental in the Hebrew language for expressing precaution and preventive fear. It is used alone or reinforced by other negative particles.
H6435.emploi: This word appears about 125 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy) and the Historical Books (Judges, Samuel, Kings). It is used to formulate divine prohibitions (Genesis 3:3), practical warnings (Proverbs 25:17: "Do not visit your neighbor's house too often, lest he become weary of you"), or military and civil orders (Deuteronomy 20:5-7: listing those who may leave the army "lest they die"). Its use is almost always linked to a serious consequence that one seeks to avoid. Over time, the meaning weakens and the word functions more as a simple conjunction particle.
H6435.portee: This word reminds us that the fear of God and caution are biblical virtues. The fear expressed by "fear that" is not panic, but vigilance that leads to obedience and self-preservation. It invites the reader to take divine warnings seriously and to anticipate the consequences of their actions — an eternal wisdom.

sens: Sweet food or cake, probably made from honey or flour
Valuable commodity that was exported and traded
H6436.detail: 1. The word designates a cooked food, most likely a pastry or cake — perhaps made from honey, flour, or oil — that was prepared as a refined dish. It is a product of culinary art, not a raw food. In Ezekiel 27:17, this pastry is listed among the goods that Judah and Israel exported to Tyre: it was valuable and sought after enough to be a commercial commodity. 2. By extension, this word evokes any luxury item or valuable good that can be exchanged advantageously. The pastry appears alongside the wheat of Minnith, honey, oil, and balm — all prestige products — indicating that it represented a wealth worthy of interest to Phoenician merchants.
H6436.origine: The Hebrew word is rare and its exact root remains uncertain, which is why even ancient translations debated it. It could be related to the idea of preparing or shaping (as one shapes dough). The Segond chose "pastry" to convey the idea of a delicately prepared and crafted food, contrasting with raw or semi-processed goods.
H6436.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:17. Ezekiel lists the treasures that Tyre received from the nations in exchange for its luxury products; the pastry is mentioned as an export from Israel, alongside wheat, honey, oil, and balm. Its uniqueness in the biblical text makes its exact meaning difficult to determine with certainty, but the context clearly shows that it is a valuable and commercial commodity.
H6436.portee: This word reminds us that in ancient Israel, as in any civilization, craftsmanship and art were employed to nourish people. The pastry here represents a gift from God, a commodity that the land of Israel could produce and offer to other peoples — a fruit of human labor acknowledging the gifts of creation.

sens: Change direction, position, or gaze
Make a U-turn, depart, withdraw
Direct one's attention or gaze towards something or someone
Transform, prepare, put in order
Incline morally or spiritually towards evil or towards good
H6437G.detail:
1. To turn primarily means to physically change direction or position: one turns their body, one turns to one side. In Judges 15:4, Samson "turned tail to tail" the foxes by tying them together, changing their position and direction.
2. To return or depart signifies going back on one's steps, leaving elsewhere, or turning away from a place. In Deuteronomy 1:40, the people are called to "turn and go into the wilderness," leaving the place where they were.
3. To turn one's attention or gaze towards someone or something means to direct one's eyes and heart towards them. In 2 Kings 2:24, Elisha "turned around to look at them," focusing his attention on the children who mocked him.
4. To turn can also mean to prepare or put in order, transforming a place for use: in Genesis 24:31, the servant says, "I have prepared the house," meaning he has turned it to welcome guests.
5. On a spiritual level, turning towards evil or towards good expresses the choice to turn away from God or to draw closer to Him, to disobey or to obey.
H6437G.origine: The verb הוּן (panah) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to move sideways" or "to change direction." It is a very concrete action verb, linked to the idea of bodily movement. The root has also given rise to other verbal forms depending on the context: the simple form (Qal) is the most common, but the Bible also uses reinforced forms that intensify or modulate the action of turning. This verb expresses one of the most elementary and richly metaphorical human actions.
H6437G.emploi: The verb panah appears 127 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Pentateuch, Judges, Kings) and sometimes in poetry (Psalms, Job). It is a very versatile verb: it describes the physical turning of people and objects (turning the head, turning tail to tail), the movement from one place to another (going into the wilderness, returning), and the movement of gaze or attention (looking at someone, turning around to see). Often it also carries a spiritual or moral charge: turning towards someone can mean turning towards God or turning away from Him. In Deuteronomy and in Kings, turning frequently appears in contexts of decision: the people turn to obey or to disobey. The word does not have a fixed unique meaning; its strength lies in its ability to depict the concrete gesture that opens up to meaning.
H6437G.portee: For the Christian reader, turning evokes the gesture of one who changes course, who pivots to face reality or God. The Bible uses this word to speak of repentance (turning from evil), prayer (turning towards God), and obedience (turning to follow). Each physical turn in the biblical text invites reflection on the spiritual turns of life: where am I turned? Towards whom, towards what should I turn? The simple yet eloquent word reminds us that faith is a matter of concrete direction, not abstraction.

sens: The corner or angle of a wall, building, or fortified enclosure
Figurative sense: a place of power or strategic strength
H6437H.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the corner or angle formed by two walls meeting. In the text of 2 Chronicles 25:23, it refers to the "corner gate" of Jerusalem, one of the gates of the city wall, located where the ramparts formed an angle. The four hundred cubits of breach extend from the Ephraim gate to this corner gate.
2. By extension, the word can evoke a strategic point, as the angles of fortifications were key positions: this is where defenses were reinforced and monitored. The corner gate was therefore a place of power and control over the city.
H6437H.origine: The Hebrew word panah (פָּנָה) comes from a root that literally means "to turn" or "to face." The name "corner" derives naturally from this: it is the place where one turns, where the wall changes direction. The root expresses the movement of rotation or change of orientation, hence the transition to the concrete sense of "corner" or "angle." This noun belongs to the same lexical family as other Hebrew words expressing turning or changing direction.
H6437H.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible in this usage. It specifically designates a fortified gate of Jerusalem, the "corner gate," mentioned in the account of the siege of the city by Joash, king of Israel. The context is military: Joash breached a gap in the wall between the Ephraim gate and the corner gate, thus demonstrating his control over the capital of the kingdom of Judah. This architectural and fortified technical term reflects the strategic importance of angles in the urban defenses of the time.
H6437H.portee: This term reminds us that in the Bible, even concrete details — here the elements of a city's fortification — serve to tell the story of God's judgment on His people. The corner gate, through which Joash enters Jerusalem, marks the humiliation of the kingdom of Judah before the kingdom of Israel. It is a lesson on the consequences of unfaithfulness: the defenses that God protected are broken, and places of strength become places of defeat.

sens: Corner or junction point of two walls or two lines that meet
Point of fortification or access in a city wall
H6438G.detail:
1. The word designates the place where two surfaces meet at a right angle, particularly at the corners of walls or buildings. In 2 Chronicles 26:9, Uzziah builds towers "on the corner" of the wall of Jerusalem, meaning at its intersection points. It is a precise geographical and architectural landmark.
2. In the context of urban fortifications, the corner is a strategic place where two sections of wall intersect, often reinforced by a gate or a tower. In 2 Kings 14:13, Joash "made a breach of four hundred cubits in the wall of Jerusalem, from the Ephraim gate to the corner gate": this last landmark designates a well-known and visible position in the city, a point of reference for both inhabitants and attackers.
H6438G.origine: The Hebrew word pinna comes from a root meaning "to turn" or "to face": an angle is where something diverts or changes direction. This same root produces other words to designate points of break or turns. The word appears in the context of architecture and urban geography, fields where angles are important structural elements.
H6438G.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided biblical usages, always to describe the walls and gates of Jerusalem. It designates fixed and recognizable reference points: a corner gate (2 Kings 14:13 and Jeremiah 31:38) or a fortified corner (2 Chronicles 26:9). These three passages show that "the corner" was a well-identified landmark in the topography of Jerusalem, well-known enough to serve as a reference in descriptions of fortifications, destructions, or reconstructions. The term remains stable in its concrete and geographical sense.
H6438G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the material details of the Bible — the stones, the walls, the exact measurements — are not vain ornaments: they anchor the story of God's people in a tangible geographical reality. Seeing Jerusalem defended, rebuilt, its corners fortified, is to contemplate God's faithfulness to His city and His people, even through trials.

sens: Corner or edge of a square or rectangular object
Angle of a city or territory, peripheral region
Main point or peak, dominant position
Character of power or authority (figurative image)
H6438H.detail:
1. The corner or angle of a building, base, or altar: the meeting of two surfaces forming a projection. In Exodus 27:2, the altar must have horns at its four "corners"; in 1 Kings 7:34, the bases of the temple have prominent "angles."

2. The angle of a city or the corner of a region, as a limit or place set apart. In Nehemiah 3:31, the reconstruction of the walls passes through a "high chamber of the corner"; in Proverbs 25:24, staying at the corner of a roof means withdrawing to the side rather than enduring a quarrelsome woman.

3. The main or chief stone that holds the structure: the foundational angle. In Psalm 118:22, the stone rejected by the builders becomes the chief of the "corner" — in other words, the stone that crowns or establishes the work.

4. In a figurative sense, the chief, the guide, the one who leads: as the corner of the building supports its structure. Zechariah 10:4 calls the Lord the "corner peg" of the people, the one who supports them.
H6438H.origine: The Hebrew word pinnah comes from a root expressing the idea of point or projection. It primarily designates the physical, visible, and tangible corner — the place where two lines meet at a right angle. By extension, it applies to what is extreme, remarkable, or dominant: the chief who "supports" like a cornerstone. This architectural image is frequent in biblical texts to speak of power or stability.
H6438H.emploi: The word appears 26 times, mainly in historical and poetic books. Literally, it designates the angles and corners of constructed objects: the altar (Exodus), the bases of the temple (1 Kings, Ezekiel), the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah). In poetry, it takes on a figurative hue: one who withdraws to the corner of the roof for peace (Proverbs); the cornerstone of Psalm 118:22, a messianic keystone; the chief or guide as the "corner" of the people (Zechariah). The context (constructive or personal) determines whether the word remains concrete or takes on a symbolic significance.
H6438H.portee: The cornerstone of Psalm 118:22, rejected and then made chief, is the great Christological image of the New Testament: it speaks of Christ, despised yet fundamental for the edifice of salvation. More broadly, the word invites the believer to see that what seems worthless — a corner, an edge, a humble position — can be precisely what supports and holds the whole together. It is a lesson of faith: true strength often lies where one least expects it.

sens: Place where Jacob wrestled with God and was renamed Israel
Location near the Jabbok, on the northern bank, close to the Jordan
Fortified city that Gideon destroyed
Place that King Jeroboam rebuilt
H6439G.detail:
1. Penuel is the name that Jacob gave to the place where he spent the night wrestling with a divine being, a decisive event in his life (Genesis 32:30). The name literally means "face of God": Jacob himself explains that he has "seen God face to face" at this location and that he was spared. It is a moment of intimate and transformative encounter with the divine.
2. Geographically, Penuel was a specific site located near the Jabbok, the river that marks the boundary between the lands east and west of the Jordan (Genesis 32:31). The sun rose when Jacob left after that memorable night.
3. Many centuries later, Penuel had become a fortified city. Gideon, pursuing the Midianite kings, went there and asked its inhabitants for supplies; when refused, he swore to tear down the city's tower (Judges 8:8-9) and kept his word by destroying it (Judges 8:17).
4. King Jeroboam I later rebuilt Penuel as one of his main strongholds after the division of the kingdom of Israel (1 Kings 12:25), restoring it to political and military significance.
H6439G.origine: The Hebrew name פְּנוּאֵל (Penuel) is composed of "pnè" (face) and "èl" (God): "the face of God" or "face towards God." It is a meaningful name given by Jacob himself to commemorate his extraordinary encounter with the divine. The same site is sometimes referred to as Peniel (פְּנִיאֵל) in the Bible, a spelling variant of the same Hebrew name.
H6439G.emploi: Penuel appears 6 times in the Bible. First, it is the place of Jacob's night vision (Genesis 32:30-31), the pivotal moment of his story. Then, Penuel reappears during the time of the Judges as a city in Gilead, east of the Jordan, through which Gideon passed while pursuing the Midianites (Judges 8:8-9, 8:17). Finally, King Jeroboam made it a fortified center of the young northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:25), marking the site's lasting strategic importance. The usages show that Penuel was a major geographical crossroads and a political stake over the centuries.
H6439G.portee: The name Penuel reminds the reader that the spiritual life of God's people has deep roots: it goes back to Jacob's intimate encounter with the Lord. This place, sanctified by Jacob's vision, becomes a witness to God's action in history, from the deliverance brought by Gideon to political and military resurrections. For every believer, Penuel evokes the possibility of a transformative encounter with God, even in the midst of struggle and uncertainty.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Hur
Father of Gedor
H6439H.detail: Penuel is a man of the tribe of Judah, son of Hur (who was himself the son of Ephrath) and brother of several other sons of Hur: Uri, Shobal, Salma, Hareph, Jezreel, Ishma, Idbash, Hazzelelponi, and Ezer (1 Chronicles 4:4). He is known as the father of Gedor. Nothing else is known about his life; he appears only in the genealogy of Judah at the time of the settlement in Egypt and the wilderness.
H6439H.origine: The name Penuel literally means "face of God" or "face to face with God" (Hebrew: פְּנֵי "pnei" = face, visage, and אֵל "el" = God). This name recalls the place where Jacob, in the Genesis account, wrestled with God and received the name Israel, naming the place Peniel "for I have seen God face to face." Although this Penuel of Judah is a different person from the place, the name reflects the theological significance of "encounter with God."
H6439H.emploi: Penuel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:4, in the genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as the son of Hur (the firstborn of Ephrath, father of Bethlehem) and father of Gedor. His inclusion in this genealogy indicates that he held an established place in the lineage of Judah, although the details of his personal life are not reported to us. The genealogical context suggests that he lived during the time of Egypt and the wilderness.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H6439I.detail: Pénuel is a man belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in Scripture. He is the son of Shashak and the brother of several other Benjamites, including Jiphdéja. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy, a period when the kingdom of Israel had split into two kingdoms.
H6439I.origine: The name Pénuel (or Péniel) means "face of God" or "seeing God." It comes from two Hebrew words: "pne" (face, front) and "el" (God). This same name originally designated a place in Transjordan where Jacob wrestled with God at night (Genesis 32:30), which explains its theophanic significance. The name was then borne by several distinct individuals in Israel's history.
H6439I.emploi: Pénuel appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:25, where he is listed among the sons of Shashak in the genealogy of Benjamin. This passage is part of a detailed genealogical list of Benjaminite family leaders, likely reconstructed after the Babylonian exile. His unique mention suggests that he was a figure of lesser importance in Israel's history, but notable enough to be preserved in the official genealogical records.

sens: front part of the head, seat of the eyes, nose, and mouth
physical presence of a person
surface of a thing or the ground
forward direction, movement forward
in front of something, in an anterior position in space or time
H6440G.detail:
1. The face is literally the front part of the human (or animal) head. When Scripture speaks of seeing the "face" of the king in 2 Samuel 14:32, it refers to meeting him in person, having access to his presence.
2. By extension, the "face" designates the person themselves, their concrete existence. To say that something is done "before" someone ("before God" in Genesis 6:11) means that that person is aware of it, sees it, and is responsible for it.
3. The face can also be the visible surface of something — thus the face of the ground, the earth itself.
4. Used adverbially, the word takes on the meaning of "forward," of movement or progression forward.
5. As a preposition, "before" situates a person or thing in relation to another: before in a spatial sense ("before you" in Joshua 2:10, the water recedes), or before in the sense of presence and personal relationship ("before the Lord" means under God's gaze, in His presence, responsible to Him).
H6440G.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "turning" or "going towards." The face is therefore literally what turns towards, what is in front. The same word in Hebrew serves to designate both the physical face, personal presence, and forward direction. This versatility comes from the primary image: one meets someone face to face, one has their face before them, and thus one is in their presence.
H6440G.emploi: This word appears more than a thousand times in the Hebrew Bible — it is one of the most frequent words. It is first used literally for the face, animal or human (Genesis 1:29 and passim). But very quickly, it develops a relational sense: being "before" God is not just a spatial position, it is a moral and spiritual reality (Genesis 6:11: the corrupt earth before the Lord). The word is also used to express past time ("formerly," "long ago"), as a sort of temporal direction towards the past. In the narratives of Genesis especially, "before" constantly recurs to mark relationships between characters and between man and God: it is a fundamental word to express presence, responsibility, and the order of things.
H6440G.portee: For the Christian reader, this word speaks to the reality of the divine gaze. When the Bible says that something is done "before God," it reminds us that nothing is hidden, that God sees everything — it is an invitation to live in awareness of His presence. Moreover, the word emphasizes that the relationship with God is a face-to-face encounter, a personal matter: it is not abstract, it is concrete and engaging.

sens: The front part of the head, from the hairline to the chin
The expression or appearance of the face
The person themselves, considered in their identity or presence
The front, the surface, or the visible aspect of something
The presence or being of someone, particularly face to face
In front of, ahead of, or towards the front side (spatial or temporal sense)
H6440H.detail:
1. The face is primarily the front part of the head, from the forehead to the chin. It is the concrete visage that expresses feelings and allows one to recognize someone (Ecclesiastes 8:1: "The wisdom of a man makes his face shine").

2. The word also refers to the expression of the face, the way one appears: this is why the face can be bright or stern, anxious or serene, reflecting the state of the soul.

3. By extension, the face represents the person themselves in their living presence, especially when speaking of presenting oneself or hiding from someone. Hiding "far from the face" of God (Genesis 3:8) means hiding far from His presence.

4. The word is also used for the visible surfaces of things: the face of the earth (Numbers 12:3) refers to the earth's surface itself.

5. Finally, "face" can simply denote presence or being: "Will you hide your face?" (Psalms 13:2) means "Will you be absent?", will you turn away from me?

6. In a spatial or temporal sense, the face indicates direction, the front, or what is ahead: "You shall turn your face toward Jerusalem" (Ezekiel 4:7) means to orient one's attention toward; "before the face" of someone means in their presence or toward them.
H6440H.origine: The Hebrew word פָּנֶה comes from a root that suggests the movement of turning or direction. The face is literally what one sees first when looking at someone, hence its use to denote presence in person. The word has a wide range of uses as it is rooted in a very basic image of human life: the face as the seat of identity, as what is shown or hidden, as what looks toward something. This richness has led to very frequent prepositional and adverbial uses in Hebrew.
H6440H.emploi: The word פָּנֶה is one of the most common in the Bible, used 373 times. It appears in all books, from Genesis to the last prophets. In its primary sense, it denotes the physical face of humans and even celestial beings (the cherubim have a face, Exodus 25:20). It is used to express emotion or judgment: a shining face, a stern face, a changed face. But very often, especially in theological contexts, it denotes the personal presence of God: being "before the face of God" or hiding "far from His face" expresses the immediate experience of the relationship with Him, a presence that cannot be escaped or neglected. The word also takes on prepositional and adverbial meanings: "before," "in front of," "ahead" (temporally), often introduced by other prepositions. This is its most frequent use in biblical prose, where it serves to structure the space and time of the narrative.
H6440H.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not conceal the face but makes it visible. The face is the place of relationship: that with others (looking at each other face to face), and especially that with God. When Scripture speaks of the face of God, it does not describe a material form, but expresses the reality of a living, personal, and unavoidable presence. Hiding one's face means turning away; showing one's face means coming to meet. This image invites us not to reduce our relationship with God to the abstract or the invisible, but to live it as an authentic face-to-face encounter, as one truly meets someone they look at directly.

sens: The face or front of a person or thing
The presence of someone
The reason, the motive for which something happens or someone acts
In front of, ahead, nearby
The surface or appearance
H6440I.detail:
1. The face or front of a person or thing: the word primarily denotes the physical face, the figure. This image is retained even when the word takes on a more abstract meaning.
2. The presence of someone: when speaking of "the face" or "before" someone, it evokes being in their presence, face to face with them. It is being before their eyes.
3. The reason, the motive: this is the most common meaning in our translations. When a calamity occurs "because of" wickedness (Jeremiah 4:4), the Hebrew word evokes the idea that the wickedness stands "before" God, it is visible, it provokes His reaction. The motive is what "justifies" or "precedes" the action.
4. In front of, ahead, nearby: the word can also simply mean "in front of" in the sense of direction or location, "toward the front".
5. The surface or appearance: sometimes the word denotes what is seen from the outside, the external aspect of something.
H6440I.origine: The Hebrew word פָּנֶה (pâneh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "turning" or "turning toward." Its primary meaning is the face, that which faces. From there, the idea of "presence" has developed naturally: your face is you in person. Then, by extension, "that which is before you" — a motive, a reason — as if this reason stands "before" and justifies the action. It is a very ancient Semitic image where the cause is figuratively represented as that which "precedes" or "faces."
H6440I.emploi: The word פָּנֶה appears 79 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narrative prose and in laments. The dominant meaning is that of "cause" or "motive": Rebecca is disgusted with life "because of" the daughters of Heth (Genesis 27:46), Jeremiah calls for circumcision "lest my anger break out... because of" wickedness (Jeremiah 4:4), Joshua finds courage "because of" the fear that the Canaanites have of Israel (Joshua 2:24). It is also encountered as a preposition meaning "before" or "in the presence of." In Job 37:19, the word seems to mean "ignorant," translating another nuance: being "without face" can mean "not daring to present oneself." The context always determines which meaning is retained.
H6440I.portee: Understanding that the Bible uses the word "cause" in a very embodied way helps the reader grasp that the motives behind divine or human actions are never abstract: they stand "before" God like a visible face. God reacts to wickedness not as a distant judge, but as someone face to face with what is happening. This invites the Christian to see that their actions are never hidden, but always "before" the gaze of God, and that the reason why they experience judgment or not is always readable, always motivated by what is presented to that gaze.

sens: The front of the face, from the eyes to the chin
The presence of a person, their being considered face to face
The visible surface of a thing, of land, of a region
The front, what is turned towards, the direction of
In the past, formerly (when 'face' marks time)
H6440J.detail:
1. The front of the human face, the part where the features appear: it is the seat of gaze and expression. This meaning remains literal in many biblical contexts.
2. The person themselves, considered as present before someone else. To say 'in front of' often means 'in the presence of' or 'under the gaze of'. For example, in Exodus 33:16, being distinguished from other peoples 'in your face' means being before God Himself.
3. The top, the surface: that of a field, of a region, of the entire earth. Genesis 1:2 speaks of 'the surface of the deep'; Psalms 104:30, of the 'face of the earth' that is renewed. It is also the ground on which one walks, the visible expanse.
4. What faces, the forward direction, the orientation towards. Joshua 13:25 mentions Rabba 'facing', marking a direction of confrontation or location.
5. The past time, antiquity: 'face to face' can denote a succession or a situation 'from the beginning'.
H6440J.origine: Fundamental Hebrew root that evokes 'to turn towards' and 'to look face to face'. The word primarily designates the face, the seat of direct relationship between two beings. It extends to any surface or expanse that one sees before oneself, then to the notion of front, presence, direction. This polysemy is natural in Hebrew: what is seen, what presents itself, what looks.
H6440J.emploi: A very frequent word in the Hebrew Bible (98 occurrences here), especially in Genesis, historical narratives, and Psalms. It is first used in the concrete sense: the face of a person, of an animal, the surface of the earth (Genesis 1:2, 8:13). It also becomes an expression of location: 'in front of', 'before', 'facing' (Joshua 13:25). It can denote the formidable presence of a power, notably of God: 'in the face of the Lord' means not only 'before Him' but 'confronted with Him'. Finally, in temporal context or with preposition, it marks the front, the anteriority, the past existence. The word embraces nuances according to its context, from anatomy to theology.
H6440J.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp how the Bible conceives the relationship with God: the 'face' of the Lord is not a form, but the reality of His personal and direct presence. Speaking of 'face to face' reveals that God does not remain distant, abstract; there is encounter, mutual gaze, living word. This is also why seeking 'the face' of God in the Psalms expresses the desire for His living presence, not a mere idea.

sens: the anterior part of the head
the visible or anterior surface of a thing
the front, the forward part of a place
the presence, the proximity of someone
in the direction of, towards
formerly, in the past
H6440K.detail:
1. The face is the anterior part of the head, turned forward. It is the face with its distinctive features.
2. By extension, it is the visible or anterior surface of any object or place — the face of a field, of a mountain, of the desert. In Genesis 23:17, the field 'facing Mamre' designates its surface oriented towards that place.
3. The face also means the front, the forward part of a space. Thus, when it is said that a place is 'in front of the desert' (1 Samuel 26:1), it indicates its frontal position relative to that space.
4. Metaphorically, the face becomes personal presence: 'in front of someone' means 'in their presence', 'before them'.
5. The word also serves as an adverb or preposition to indicate direction: 'towards' or 'in the direction of'.
6. Rarely, it also evokes the past time: 'formerly', 'in ancient times', as what is 'before' oneself in time is the past.
H6440K.origine: The word פָּנֶה (pané) comes from a root that fundamentally means 'to turn' or 'to turn oneself'. The face is what turns forward, what is exposed and visible. The same root produces verbs and nouns related to 'movement' and 'direction'. It is a very ancient word in the Semitic vocabulary, first designating a very concrete and physical reality before extending to more figurative and spatial uses.
H6440K.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the provided usages, especially in the genealogical and land possession narratives of Genesis (4 occurrences related to the field of Machpelah 'facing Mamre'), as well as in texts of territorial delimitation or geographical positioning (Joshua 19:11: 'before Jokneam'). In 1 Samuel 26:1, the hill of Hakila is 'in front of the desert'. In 1 Kings, the term designates the position of a place or a person in relation to a landmark. The usage is predominantly spatial and descriptive: it situates, it localizes, it orients.
H6440K.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, geography and positioning in space are never neutral: they evoke presence, proximity, relationship to the other. When Abraham buries his wife 'facing Mamre', it is not an empty detail — it affirms where the tomb is located, on which territory, in relation to which landmarks. For the reader, this engages a worldview where everything, every person has its place and orientation.

sens: Front surface of the head, with the features of the face
The person themselves, the presence of someone (by synecdoche)
Surface or front of a thing
Position in front of someone, ahead, before
Disposition to seek, the moment when one looks forward
H6440L.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the physical face, the visage: 'Why would he see your face more dejected than that of the young men?' (Daniel 1:10), where it concerns the visible appearance of the features.
2. By natural extension, the face represents the person themselves. 'I will deliver you into the hands of those before whom you tremble' (Jeremiah 22:25): here 'before' means in presence of, face to face.
3. The word also applies to the surface of things: the face of the earth, the face of a building.
4. Used with prepositions, it expresses the spatial idea of being ahead, in presence: 'before' (in front of), 'ahead' (previously). 'The Lord... has brought him before me' (Genesis 27:20).
5. In idiomatic constructions, it takes nuanced meanings: 'to implore' someone amounts to 'to plead their face' (Psalms 119:58: 'I implore you with all my heart'), that is to turn towards them with insistence.
H6440L.origine: The Hebrew word פָּנֶה comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning towards, of presenting oneself face to face. In Hebrew, the 'face' is the seat of expression and personal presence: it is through the face that one shows oneself. Hence its extended usage to designate the person themselves, the presence. The prepositional forms of the word ('before', 'ahead') arise from this image of face-to-face interaction.
H6440L.emploi: The word appears 95 times in the Old Testament, especially in contexts of interpersonal relationship, attitude towards God, or spatial position. Used for the face itself: Daniel 1:10. For presence or person: Jeremiah 22:25 ('before whom you tremble'). With the meaning of imploring: 2 Chronicles 33:12 ('he implored the Lord'), Psalms 119:58 ('I implore you'). As an adverb or preposition: 'before' in the spatial sense (Genesis 27:20, Deuteronomy 20:3). Its meaning evolves according to the context: it can be literal (face) or fixed (position, presence, supplication), showing how in Hebrew the face embodies personal relationship.
H6440L.portee: For the biblical reader, this word reminds us that in the Bible, the face is much more than physical appearance: it is the sign of presence and relationship. 'To see the face' of God or the king is to be admitted into their presence. To plead with someone 'face to face' or 'before' them is to present oneself with sincerity. This word invites us to understand that relationships, with God as with others, rest on a real and personal presence, not abstract.

sens: The face, the figure of a person or a creature
The expression of the face, which reveals emotional state or attitude
The presence or the person itself
The appearance or surface of a thing
Toward, in the direction of, in front of (locative or temporal sense)
H6440M.detail:
1. The face is primarily the entirety of the face, the physical figure: it is the part of the head that includes the eyes, nose, mouth, and forehead. In Genesis 4:5, after Cain presented his offering, "his face fell" — we see physically on his face the disappointment and sadness.
2. The face also expresses what is happening in the heart: joy, anger, favor, disappointment. Still in Genesis 4:5, God did not look with "favor" on Cain — the face here shows what someone thinks of him, their judgment, their attitude. In Jeremiah 3:12, God says, "I will not look on you with anger": He will not welcome you with a threatening or angry face.
3. By extension, the face can designate the person themselves or their presence: "to appear before the face of God" means to present oneself before God, to enter into His presence.
4. The face or surface of a thing: the surface of the ground, the sky, the water.
5. Finally, pâneh is also used adverbially to indicate direction, movement forward: "before," "in front of," "facing." This last meaning comes from the primary sense of what is "face to face."
H6440M.origine: The Hebrew root pâneh (פנה) primarily means "to turn toward" or "to face." The word pâneh (פָּנֶה, the face) naturally derives from this: it is the part of the body that turns toward someone, that faces. The same root gives verbs like "to turn," "to direct toward." The face being what turns and presents itself first, the word has acquired the meanings of "presence," "direction," "before."
H6440M.emploi: Pâneh (face) is one of the most frequently used words in the Hebrew Bible, appearing hundreds of times. It appears in all genres of texts: historical (Genesis), prophetic (Jeremiah), poetic (Psalms). Its meanings unfold according to the context. When it literally describes a human or animal face, it speaks of physiognomy. When it follows a verb like "to look" or "to cast a look," it becomes the expression of judgment or favor: it is the attitude, the welcome. Very often, "the face of God" or "to see the face of God" refers to divine presence, access to God, or communion with Him. In Genesis 4:5 and Jeremiah 3:12, the two provided uses illustrate this interplay between the literal sense (Cain's fallen face) and the figurative sense (God's severe or benevolent gaze, in other words, His attitude, His disposition).
H6440M.portee: Understanding that the face reveals the heart invites the Christian to examine their own expressions, their reactions, but especially to meditate on "the face of God" — how He sees us, what attitude He has toward us. In moments of discouragement like Cain, we may fear God's "severe face"; but Jeremiah 3:12 reminds us that God says to Israel: "I will not look on you with anger." This is a promise: despite our unfaithfulness, His face can turn toward us with mercy, not with anger. The face of God, in the New Testament, is fully manifested in Jesus Christ.

sens: The front part of the head, from the forehead to the chin
Gaze, expression of the face
Physical presence of a person
Favor, kindness toward someone
External appearance, surface
Before, direction or place located in front
H6440N.detail:
1. The face is literally the front part of the head: it is the face with its features. In 2 Kings 9:32, one "lifts the face toward the window" to look at something, just as one lifts their head.

2. The face also expresses the inner attitude: to lift a face without blemish (Job 11:15) means to regain pride and dignity after misfortune, for it is through the face that one shows honor or shame.

3. The face represents the person themselves: to regard the face of someone means to take into account who they are, to show respect or partiality according to their status (Deuteronomy 16:19: "you shall not show partiality in judgment").

4. To face someone or "to grant face" means to show them favor, kindness: in Genesis 19:21, God says, "I grant you this grace," where the received face signifies the favor obtained.

5. The face can simply designate the surface of a thing, the external aspect that one sees first.

6. In the local or temporal sense, "face" indicates the forward direction, the front, or the notion of presence before someone: "before," "in the presence of," "approaching."
H6440N.origine: The Hebrew word פָּנֶה (pānim in plural) fundamentally designates the visible and outward-facing part, the face. It comes from an archaic root meaning "to turn" or "to turn toward": the face is what one turns toward others. The plural pānim ("faces") is often used in the singular in French to refer to the face of a single person. It is the key word to express divine or human favor: to obtain the "face" of God is to receive His kindness.
H6440N.emploi: This word appears 34 times in the provided biblical passages, especially in the wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs), historical narratives, and the Law. Its uses are clearly divided: in the literal sense (face, features), it is found in narratives (2 Kings 9:32: "to lift the face toward the window"). In the sense of person or respect due to the person, it is very common in laws regarding just judgment: Deuteronomy 16:19 prohibits showing "partiality in judgment," meaning to judge according to social status. In the sense of favor, Genesis 19:21 uses the expression "to grant face," which means to grant grace. Job 42:8 shows a very fine usage: God treats Job with "regard," meaning with particular honor, because of his virtue. The word thus glides from the concrete to the moral and relational.
H6440N.portee: This word teaches that God sees each person with equity, without regard to appearance or status: it is a call to just justice (Deuteronomy 16:19, Proverbs 24:23). For the believer, the "face" of God is the mark of His favor and presence. Finally, the word reminds us that we are visible beings, known by God who sees our heart: no lie can hide our face from the One who judges us.

sens: The part inside, the space found within a place or building
Towards the inside, in the direction of the interior
Inside rather than outside, speaking of what is hidden or protected
Then, after that (less frequent temporal value)
H6441.detail:
1. The part inside, the space found within a place or building: this word simply designates what is enclosed, contained within something. In Solomon's Temple, certain parts were covered in gold "inside" (1 Kings 6:30), that is, in the closed rooms at the heart of the building, while others were outside.
2. Towards the inside, in the direction of the interior: the word can indicate a movement or a location turned towards the heart of a space. When the blood of the sacrifice had not been brought "into the interior of the sanctuary" (Leviticus 10:18), it means that it had not been taken to the heart of the holy place, but had remained outside.
3. Inside rather than outside, speaking of what is hidden or protected: in contrast to the outside, this emphasizes the secret or reserved nature of what is inside. The porch of the Temple was "internally" covered in pure gold (2 Chronicles 3:4), highlighting the hidden wealth at the heart of the building.
4. Then, after that: in a single usage (2 Chronicles 29:18), the word takes on a temporal value to mark a succession of events, as if moving "inside" from one stage to the next.
H6441.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "face" or "front," hence the primitive meaning of "face to face" then "directly towards" and finally "towards the inside." It is a preposition formed with the suffix -ah that reinforces the idea of direction or location. The word is related to the notion of "penimim" (inner faces) and naturally opposes "externally" or "outside." This root is very ancient in Hebrew and appears in the architectural descriptions of the Temple.
H6441.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in passages that describe Solomon's Temple and its precise dimensions (1 Kings 6 and 2 Chronicles 3), as well as in the vision of the future Temple in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 40-41). It is also used in the laws of worship (Leviticus 10:18) to indicate where certain parts of the sacrifice must be taken. The word is also found in poetry (Psalms 45:14, describing the inner beauty of the king's bride). In all these contexts, it retains its fundamental spatial meaning: the inside in relation to the outside, the interior in relation to the exterior. Only once, in 2 Chronicles 29:18, does it take on a temporal nuance to mean "then."
H6441.portee: This word reminds us that the Temple had an inside and an outside, a hidden sacredness and limited access. For the reader, it emphasizes how biblical worship distinguished spaces according to their proximity to the presence of God: certain places remained forbidden to the uninitiated. This spatial contrast between "inside" and "outside" helps to understand the importance of the veil that separated the sacred spaces and how God established protective boundaries around His worship.

sens: That which is within, in the internal part of a building or space
Belonging to what is hidden, secret, reserved for some
Concerning the soul, the heart, the spiritual life
H6442.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the interior space of a building, in contrast to what is exterior. In Solomon's temple, the "cherubim" are placed "in the interior" of the house (1 Kings 6:27), that is, in the central part of the sanctuary. Ezekiel measures the "inner court" of the temple (Ezekiel 40:19), the courtyard that is inside the temple enclosure.
2. By extension, the word qualifies what is reserved, hidden, or forbidden to the common: Queen Esther must pass through "the inner gate" (Ezekiel 8:3) to enter the secret apartments of the palace, or the "inner chambers" (1 Chronicles 28:11) of the temple that are not accessible to all.
3. In a more spiritual sense, the word can designate what belongs to the hidden realm of the soul or conscience, what happens within a person rather than what is seen outside.
H6442.origine: The Hebrew word פְּנִימִי (péniymi) comes from the root פנים (panim), which literally means "face" or "front," but also "interior" or "that which is turned inward." This root is very common in Hebrew and gives rise to many words related to the idea of presence, direct relation, and interiority. The suffix -י (-i) makes it an adjective: "that which is interior, that which belongs to the inside."
H6442.emploi: This word appears about 29 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the architectural descriptions of Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6-7) and in the vision of Ezekiel's temple (Ezekiel 40-46). It serves to distinguish the interior spaces of the temple or palace from the exterior spaces. In the temple, there is an "inner court" (reserved courtyard), "inner chambers" (secret rooms), an "inner gate" (entrance leading to reserved areas). In Esther, too, "the inner gate" marks access to the king's private apartments. The usage is concrete and spatial: it is always about locating something in the interior space of a structure.
H6442.portee: This word reminds us that the temple, like the heart of the believer, has visible dimensions and hidden dimensions. The interior spaces of the temple, forbidden to ordinary people, signified the increasing holiness of the sanctuary. For the reader of Ezekiel, contemplating the vision of the "inner" temple reveals the hidden glory of God at the heart of His dwelling. This word also invites reflection on what happens within us: our thoughts, our motives, our secret communion with God are never as important as what others see.

sens: Shiny precious stone formed in shells
Object of great price and rare value
What is beautiful and precious par excellence
Comparison of beauty or moral value
H6443.detail:
1. The pearl is a precious stone found in marine shells. It is shiny and white, as shown by comparisons with snow and milk in Lamentations 4:7: the princes are "more radiant than snow, whiter than milk."
2. In the Hebrew Old Testament, pearls represent a rare and desirable wealth. In Proverbs 20:15, they are mentioned alongside gold as symbols of what is valuable on earth.
3. The pearl becomes the image of what surpasses everything in value. Wisdom is "more precious than pearls" (Proverbs 3:15), meaning it infinitely exceeds all material wealth.
4. The word also applies to the moral beauty and value of a person. A virtuous woman is "far more precious than pearls" (Proverbs 31:10): her virtue makes her more valuable than any treasure.
H6443.origine: The Hebrew word pinina likely comes from a root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." It literally refers to the pearl, a shiny stone formed naturally in marine mollusks. The term appears exclusively in biblical wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Lamentations), a context where value and beauty are discussed. It is a foreign word borrowed from the vocabularies of maritime trade and luxury.
H6443.emploi: The word pearl appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Lamentations). Each occurrence uses it as a comparative term to express supreme value. In the four passages from Proverbs (3:15, 8:11, 20:15, 31:10), the pearl serves as a reference point to affirm that wisdom and virtue surpass all earthly goods — they are worth more, they have greater value. In Job 28:18, pearls alongside coral and crystal together acknowledge that no material wealth rivals wisdom. Lamentations 4:7 uses a related word (coral) to describe the radiant beauty of the princes before the siege of Jerusalem. The image remains one of rarity, luster, and pricelessness.
H6443.portee: For the Christian reader, the pearl reminds us that wisdom and spiritual virtue infinitely surpass material wealth and appearances. This image invites a reevaluation of priorities: what shines and attracts the world — gold, possessions — is worthless compared to wisdom and righteousness. It is a biblical invitation, at the very heart of the Old Testament, to seek first the hidden treasure, that which does not rust or perish.

sens: Rival of the prophetess Hannah, second wife of Elkanah during the united monarchy in Israel
H6444.detail: Peninnah is the second wife of Elkanah, mentioned at the beginning of the account of Samuel's birth. Unlike Hannah, she has children (1 Samuel 1:2), which made her a "fulfilled" woman in the eyes of society at the time. During solemn sacrifices, Elkanah gave her portions as a fruitful wife (1 Samuel 1:4). She embodies the "happy" woman according to human criteria, capable of giving sons to her husband.
H6444.origine: Her name means "jewel" or "pearl" in Hebrew, an image of beauty and value. It is a rare name that appears only in the story of Samuel and does not appear anywhere else in the Bible. This name evokes visible wealth, external beauty, which contrasts with the hidden but decisive role that the "barren" Hannah will play in the history of Israel's salvation.
H6444.emploi: Peninnah appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Samuel 1, at the threshold of Samuel's story. She is first presented as Elkanah's co-wife, the one who "had children" when Hannah did not (1 Samuel 1:2). Then she is mentioned again during family sacrifices, receiving portions as a fruitful wife (1 Samuel 1:4). Peninnah represents the "normal," visible, and fruitful life, in contrast to Hannah's apparent sterility — but the rest of the story will reveal that it is Hannah who will give birth to Samuel, the great prophet and judge of Israel.
H6444.portee: Peninnah embodies a profound biblical lesson: what shines on the outside and seems to be visible blessing are not always signs of God's plan. Hannah, despised for her barrenness, becomes the instrument of the divine purpose, while Peninnah disappears from history. This comparison reminds us that God does not judge by appearances, and that true blessing is often that which is not visible on the surface.

sens: To raise someone with too much gentleness and complacency
To spoil through excessive indulgence
H6445.detail:
1. To treat softly means to raise a child without strictness, pampering them excessively. The word evokes the image of an upbringing that lacks firmness. In Proverbs 29:21, we see that a servant who has been treated softly from childhood ends up believing he is a son: excessive gentleness causes him to lose touch with reality and creates illusions about his place.
2. More broadly, it means to spoil someone through an inappropriate indulgence, to pamper them outrageously. Such complacency, far from forming character, weakens and corrupts it.
H6445.origine: The Hebrew verb panaḳ belongs to the family of roots that express softness and excessive delicacy. It fundamentally denotes the idea of treating with misplaced tenderness. The form used in the Bible (the Piel) intensifies the meaning, marking a repeated action or a habitual attitude of complacency.
H6445.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 29:21. The biblical usage is clearly negative: the preaching of Proverbs criticizes this excessive indulgence, showing that treating a servant softly from childhood produces confusion in him and spoils his character. It is a warning against false gentleness in education and authority.
H6445.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that true love includes correction and character formation. Spoiling someone is not loving them: it often harms them. Biblical wisdom calls for a balance between kindness and firmness, between tenderness and expectation. This is particularly relevant for parents and educators.

sens: long garment with sleeves and hem adorned with various colors
mark of high status or royal favor
sign of distinction and honor
H6446.detail:
1. It is a long-sleeved tunic with a hem embroidered in multiple colors, a garment that stands out from simple everyday clothing. The tunic that Jacob gives to Joseph in Genesis 37:3 is "of many colors" — this Hebrew word specifically denotes this diversity of shades that makes the garment visible and prestigious.
2. Wearing such a tunic meant enjoying a special position, as it was a luxury reserved for royal sons or particularly beloved children. The daughter of King Amnon also wears "a multicolored tunic," as the text specifies in 2 Samuel 13:18, "for it was the garment worn by the king's daughters."
3. The garment thus becomes a visible symbol of love and preference: Jacob loves Joseph "more than all his other sons" and gives him this tunic to express it. But this same garment also becomes an object that provokes the deadly jealousy of his brothers.
H6446.origine: The Hebrew word פַּס (pas) comes from a root meaning "to spread out" or "to unfold," an image of the fabric that is spread out to be seen entirely. It first denotes the palm of the hand or the sole of the foot — these flat surfaces that extend — and then by extension the garment that extends over the whole body, covered with multicolored patterns that "spread out" visibly.
H6446.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Bible, only in the accounts of Genesis 37 (Joseph's tunic) and 2 Samuel 13 (the tunic of Amnon's daughter, Tamar). Each occurrence emphasizes the same detail: this distinctive garment marks the wearer as someone important. For Joseph, it is the gift that expresses paternal love but triggers fraternal hatred. For Tamar, it is the privilege of the virgin daughters of the royal palace. When Tamar "tears" her tunic in 2 Samuel 13:19, it symbolizes the destruction of her honor and status.
H6446.portee: This tunic teaches us how visible signs of love and favor can become sources of jealousy if grace is not received with humility. Joseph will experience this bitterly: the garment that was meant to express his father's love will be used by his brothers to make him believe he is dead. It is a reminder that only God distributes favor according to His justice, and that marks of honor must be worn wisely, without provocation.

sens: the palm of the hand, the inner part of the hand between the wrist and the fingers
the finger or the hand itself, as an instrument of action
H6447.detail:
1. The word properly designates the palm of the hand: the fleshy inner surface that is visible when the hand is opened. It is the most sensitive and useful part for grasping, striking, writing. In the account of Daniel 5:5, it is this "end of the hand" that miraculously writes the condemnation on the wall of King Belshazzar's palace.
2. By extension, the word can refer to the whole hand or the fingers, as the palm is the active heart of the hand, by which it acts. In Daniel 5:24, God sends this "end of the hand" to write: it is the acting hand, the divine instrument of judgment against the king.
H6447.origine: The Hebrew word pas comes from a root that means "to open" or "to extend." The palm is the part of the hand that opens and extends to grasp, strike, or write. It is a concrete word, an image of the body in action. It appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible and is only used in the Aramaic accounts of Daniel.
H6447.emploi: The word appears only twice, both in Aramaic in the book of Daniel, in chapter 5, one of the most dramatic passages in the Bible. These two uses describe the mysterious hand that writes God's judgment against King Belshazzar during his profane feast. In both verses, the emphasis is on the visible action: it is this "end of the hand" that writes, that becomes visible, that accomplishes the judgment. The usage underscores the concrete and visual, almost supernatural, aspect of divine judgment.
H6447.portee: This word reminds the reader that the hand is the place of action, that it can be God's instrument to execute His judgment. In this passage, God's invisible hand writes the message that no one can ignore: it is an invitation to take divine justice seriously and not to underestimate the invisible authority that governs the history of nations.

sens: Look carefully, scan visually to know
Inspect a place by traversing it
Observe in detail to judge or appreciate
H6448.detail:
1. To examine means to look carefully to truly know something. It is to focus on every detail, as one would when inspecting a building room by room. In Psalm 48:14, the psalmist invites the faithful to examine the walls and palaces of Zion: they must look at them in detail to better remember and talk about them to future generations.
2. The word evokes the idea of traversing a space while observing it carefully. One does not merely glance: one goes through, scrutinizes, mentally visits each part. This careful examination allows one to truly know what one is looking at.
H6448.origine: The Hebrew root פָּסַג (pasag) expresses the idea of passing through or traversing. The verb in the Piel form (an intensive form) reinforces this idea: to examine is to review something with intention and attention. The word conveys a methodical inspection, a deliberate passage to better know.
H6448.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 48:14. It denotes the action of examining the fortifications and palaces of Zion. The context shows that this examination is not idle: it aims to create a memory, to be able to tell the next generation what one has seen. It is an examination that is part of the transmission of faith and knowledge of God's people.
H6448.portee: This verb invites us to a genuine attention to the works and places of God. To examine is not to remain superficial, but to take the time to truly look, to understand, and to memorize for transmission. For the Christian reader, it is a call to observe with respect and reverence the signs of God's presence, and to speak of them authentically to those who follow us.

sens: Mountain of Moab to the east of the Jordan Valley, near the Dead Sea
Summit from which Moses viewed the Promised Land before his death
H6449.detail: Pisgah is a mountain located in Moab, on the northeast shore of the Dead Sea, overlooking the Jordan Valley. It is a place of vision and transmission: Moses ascended there at the end of his life to see with his own eyes the Promised Land that he would not cross. In Deuteronomy 34:1-3, the Lord shows him "all the land" from this summit. It is also a geographical landmark: in Deuteronomy 3:17 and 4:49, it is mentioned as a boundary of the lands granted to the tribes east of the Jordan. It appears in a context of defining the borders of the territory of Israel.
H6449.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "cleft" or "chasm," likely evoking the rugged geography of this mountainous region of Moab. It is a geographical name from the biblical Levant, preserved in the Segond in its Hebrew form "Pisgah."
H6449.emploi: Pisgah appears 8 times in the Bible, always in the Old Testament and almost exclusively in the Pentateuch (5 times in Deuteronomy, 2 times in Numbers, 2 times in Joshua). It is first mentioned as a landmark in Numbers 21:20 and 23:14, where Balak brings the diviner Balaam to curse Israel. It then serves as a territorial boundary in Deuteronomy 3:17 and 4:49, marking the region of lands distributed to the transjordanian tribes. Its role culminates in Deuteronomy 3:27 and especially 34:1, where Moses ascends to contemplate the inheritance he will not possess: this vision from the summit is a decisive moment at the end of his life.
H6449.portee: Pisgah symbolizes for the reader the moment when the divine promise becomes visible, even when possession of it is denied. It is a place of faith: Moses sees and believes what God has promised, even though he dies before entering it. This summit invites every Christian to contemplate God's plans for their life, even in the face of limits and unfulfilled promises.

sens: A place in western Judea, at the border of a territory
H6450.detail: 1. Pas-Dammim literally means "boundary of blood" or "border of blood" in Hebrew. It is a location in western Judea, likely a border area where Israelites and Philistines clashed. In 1 Chronicles 11:13, it is the site of a battle where the Philistines gathered and the people fled before them, while one of David's warriors stood firm there.
H6450.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew words: "pas" (פַּס) means "boundary" or "border," and "dammim" (דַּמִּים) means "blood." This place is also known as Éphès-Dammim (אֶ֫פֶס דַּמִּים), which means "boundary of blood" or "end of blood" — two names for the same location in the region of Judea where confrontations with the Philistines were frequent.
H6450.emploi: Pas-Dammim appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:13. It is a place associated with military resistance and courage: one of David's mighty warriors stands firm there during a battle against the Philistines, while the rest of the troops flee. This site bears a name that evokes battles and spilled blood, reflecting its role in Israel's military history.

sens: wealth in quantity, profusion
H6451.detail: 1. Abundance, wealth in quantity: the word evokes a profusion, an overflowing magnitude. In Psalms 72:16, it describes the harvest of the just king that will be so generous that "the grain will be abundant in the land" — an image of prosperity and divine blessing upon the earth.
H6451.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of filling and fullness. Its exact etymology is debated by scholars, but the underlying image is one of abundance that "fills" the space, overflowing with wealth. It is a rare word in the Old Testament, which sometimes makes its precise meaning uncertain.
H6451.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 72:16. It describes the abundance of grain in the land under the reign of the just king — a messianic or ideal blessing. The context shows that this abundance is a consequence of the king's justice and God's favor.
H6451.portee: This word reminds us that God promises abundance to His people when justice reigns. It is not a promise of endless wealth, but of generous provision that meets true needs. It invites the reader to seek first the reign of justice and to trust in God's generosity.

sens: Cross an obstacle by jumping or leaping over
Spare someone, leave them unharmed
Ignore, leave aside
H6452A.detail:
1. To cross an obstacle by jumping or leaping over: this is the movement of one who jumps over something that stands in their way. At Passover in Egypt, the Lord "will pass over" the houses marked with blood: He jumps over the lintel and the doorposts, He leaps over this sign and does not enter the house (Exodus 12:13, 12:23). It is the gesture of vigilant protection.
2. To spare someone, leave them unharmed: when one passes over a house, they leave it intact. The Lord spares the firstborns of Israel by not striking them, as He strikes those of Egypt. The word evokes this active clemency, this decision not to touch (Exodus 12:27).
3. To ignore, leave aside: in Isaiah 31:5, the Lord "will spare" Jerusalem by protecting it, like a bird that spreads its wings and covers its nest, leaving it outside the lurking danger.
H6452A.origine: The word comes from the root פסח (p-s-ch), which paints the image of one who jumps or leaps over. In biblical Hebrew, the verb primarily means this physical act of jumping, and then by extension the idea of sparing or protecting by passing without striking. It is this same verb that gave its name to Passover (Pessah), the commemorative feast of the Lord's passing that spared Israel.
H6452A.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Bible: three times in the account of the plague of the firstborns in Egypt (Exodus 12:13, 12:23, 12:27), and once in Isaiah 31:5 for the protection of Jerusalem. In Exodus, the emphasis is on the visible act of the Lord's passing: He crosses the doors marked with blood without allowing the destroyer to enter. It is an act of benevolent discrimination: the Lord passes, but spares. In Isaiah, the meaning shifts towards maternal protection that spreads its wings over the city. Each time, the verb describes a salvation that rests on a visible mark: the blood in Egypt, the divine presence in Jerusalem.
H6452A.portee: This word reveals the tenderness of God's judgment. The Lord does not strike indiscriminately: He sees, He passes, He spares those who bear the sign of His covenant. For the Christian, Passover foreshadows Christ, whose shed blood marks and protects His people. This verb indicates that divine justice can also be a protection when it "passes over" our faults because of faith.

sens: To walk dragging a leg, struggling to maintain balance
To jump or move in fits and starts, without fluidity
To hesitate, to waver between two opinions or two paths
H6452B.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a physical handicap: walking unevenly on both legs. Mephibosheth remained lame after his childhood fall (2 Samuel 4:4), which marked his body permanently and visibly.
2. The verb also describes a jerky or disorganized movement: the prophets of Baal "leaped" before their altar (1 Kings 18:26), meaning they moved in awkward jumps, in the agitation of worship.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses moral or spiritual hesitation: when Elijah asks the people, "How long will you waver between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21), he reproaches them for vacillating between God and the idol, like someone who cannot decide to walk straight.
H6452B.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of hindered or unstable movement. The word belongs to a family that evokes obstacles, irregularity of movement. In biblical Hebrew, this verb describes both the walk of the lame and the lack of firmness in choice.
H6452B.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Samuel 4:4, it describes the lasting physical condition of a royal character. In 1 Kings 18:21, Elijah uses it mockingly: the people limp between two deities, unable to settle. In 1 Kings 18:26, the false prophets jump in a convulsive manner before the altar. The word thus oscillates between the description of a real handicap and the spiritual critique of moral oscillation.
H6452B.portee: This word teaches that spiritual indecision is a lack of moral health: one cannot follow both the true God and idols. The believer is called to "walk straight," with assurance and integrity, not to "limp" between two masters. It is a call to coherence and total commitment to God.

sens: The feast commemorating the deliverance from Egypt
The sacrificial animal for this feast
The sacrifice itself offered to God
The act of celebrating this feast
H6453.detail:
1. Passover is the great annual feast of Israel that commemorates the day when the Lord struck down the firstborn of Egypt and spared the houses marked with the blood of the lamb, thus liberating the people from slavery (Exodus 12:11). It is celebrated on the fourteenth day of the first month, and it annually revives this foundational event.

2. The word primarily refers to the unblemished lamb that was sacrificed for this feast: each family prepared its lamb, roasted it over the fire, and ate it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs (Exodus 12:21, Exodus 12:27).

3. It also refers to the offering itself, the sacrifice presented to the Lord in remembrance of His power and grace (Exodus 34:25). It is a cultic act that reconnects the people with their God.

4. Finally, the word designates the entirety of the festive celebration: not only the meal but also the days of celebration that followed, notably the Feast of Unleavened Bread which lasted seven days (2 Chronicles 35:17). Celebrating Passover meant gathering as a family and community to honor God and pass on the memory of His deliverance to future generations.
H6453.origine: The Hebrew word pesaḥ comes from a root meaning "to pass over" or "to spare": during the tenth plague in Egypt, the Lord "passed over" the houses of the Israelites marked with blood, sparing their firstborns. This name summarizes the entire miracle of the night of Passover. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), the word is rendered as "pascha" (πάσχα), which has given rise to the French "Pâque" and will also be applied to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God, in the New Testament.
H6453.emploi: The word pesaḥ appears about forty-six times in the Old Testament, primarily in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and in the historical books (Kings, Chronicles, Ezra). It is used to designate the very institution of the feast (Exodus 12), the prescriptions governing it (Numbers 9), the preparations for the sacrifice (Deuteronomy 16), and the historical celebrations of the people (2 Kings 23:21-23, where King Josiah solemnly restores Passover). The context shows that it is a rite of major importance, renewed each year, to which all Israel was required to participate or from which they were expressly excluded (Numbers 9:6-14 specifies cases of impurity or absence). Passover is both a historical memorial and an act of worship addressed to the Lord.
H6453.portee: Passover reminds the people of God that their freedom, life, and salvation come solely from divine grace. It teaches that the transition from slavery to freedom comes through shed blood, divine protection, and an act of faith: this is the central image of redemption. For the Christian, Passover takes on a new and definitive meaning in Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God whose shed blood on the cross fulfills and transforms all the Passover sacrifices of the Old Testament (1 Corinthians 5:7).

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H6454G.detail: Paseach is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned as the son of Eschthon and brother of Beth-rapha and Thechinna (1 Chronicles 4:12). His name, which means "the one who limps," was also borne by an ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. A Paseach also appears during the time of Nehemiah as the father of Jehoiada, who participated in the repair of the wall of Jerusalem.
H6454G.origine: The name Paseach literally means "the one who limps" or "the one who has a defect." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of walking with difficulty, limping.
