This type of descriptive name was common in Israel, where names often reflected a physical characteristic, a circumstance of birth, or a trait of the bearer.
H6454G.emploi: Paseach primarily designates a man from the tribe of Judah living during the divided monarchy, son of Eschthon and brother of Beth-rapha (1 Chronicles 4:12). The name Paseach is also attached to an ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, according to genealogical lists. A third Paseach, the father of Jehoiada, is mentioned in the context of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. These different occurrences of the same name show that it was a fairly common Hebrew name in the genealogies of the people of Judah.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah, ancestor of a family of temple servants
Father of Jehoiada, who helped in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem
H6454H.detail: Paseach is a proper name designating a man who lived during the time of the Exile and the Return. He first appears in the list of families that returned from exile with Zerubbabel: his descendants are mentioned among the sons of Uzza and the sons of Besaï (Ezra 2:49), and the same genealogy is found in Nehemiah 7:51. He is an ancestor of a family of temple servants. The name literally means "the one who limps" or "lame," an image that may evoke a physical infirmity or a significant event, although the Bible does not specify anything about the character himself beyond his genealogical role.
H6454H.origine: The name Paseach comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to limp" or "to be lame." The same Hebrew root appears in the word Pessah (Passover), where the image of hastily walking or a particular gait applies to the hurried passing over the houses in Egypt. It is a descriptive name, fairly common in Hebrew where names evoke physical characteristics or events.
H6454H.emploi: Paseach appears twice in the Bible, always in genealogical lists of the return from exile. In Ezra 2:49, his descendants are seen among the families of temple servants who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel after the fall of Jerusalem. This same list is reproduced in Nehemiah 7:51 with minor variations. These mentions show that Paseach's family played an administrative and religious role in the worship of the restored temple, being part of those specialized groups in the service of the sanctuary.

sens: Man who lived during the exile and the return
Father of Joiada, who restored the gate of Jerusalem
H6454I.detail: Paseach is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:6, where his son Joiada participates in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile (circa 445 B.C.). The name "Paseach" literally means "the one who limps" or "the one who has a defect," which could refer to a physical characteristic or a family nickname. Paseach belongs to a family of temple servants who had been deported with the Judeans and who return with Zerubbabel to participate in the restoration of Jerusalem.
H6454I.origine: The name Paseach comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to limp" or "to present a defect" — the same verb found to describe a limp or an imperfection. This etymological meaning suggests that the name was either a descriptive nickname or a hereditary family designation. The name belonged to a lineage of temple workers, placing the family among the Levites or servants dedicated to divine service.
H6454I.emploi: Paseach appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:6, where he is identified as the father of Joiada. The text mentions him in the context of the restoration lists of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. Paseach himself does not participate in the work — it is his son who is named among the workers. This brief mention shows that Paseach was a man established in Jerusalem after the return from exile, from a family serving in the temple, and that he had a son notable enough to be counted among the builders of the city.

sens: Who cannot walk or walks with difficulty, having a disability in the legs or feet
Who is crippled, maimed, or mutilated in a limb
Figuratively: that which is weak, defective, or ineffective
H6455.detail: 1. A lame person is someone affected by a disability that impacts their ability to walk normally. In Leviticus 21:18, those who "have a physical defect" and cannot approach the sanctuary are listed: "a blind man, a lame man, one with a flat nose." Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel 9:13 was "lame in both feet," unable to move by himself. 2. The term also applies to someone suffering from a mutilation or a more general handicap: in Deuteronomy 15:21, a "lame" animal is refused for worship, just as a "blind" animal is rejected. 3. Figuratively, the image of the lame describes what is deficient or ineffective: a proverb states that "a word out of place is like the legs of a lame man" (Proverbs 26:7), meaning it goes nowhere, it bears no fruit.
H6455.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "lameness" or "limping." It belongs to the family of words describing disabilities and physical defects. The primary meaning is very physical and concrete: the inability to place the foot firmly, to walk with a regular and assured step.
H6455.emploi: This word appears about thirteen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the laws (Leviticus, Deuteronomy), historical narratives (Samuel, where Mephibosheth is presented as lame), and prophecies (Jeremiah, Isaiah, Malachi). In the Law, the lame are excluded from service in worship (Leviticus 21:18) and lame animals cannot be offered as sacrifices (Deuteronomy 15:21, Malachi 1:8). But in the prophecies, especially in Isaiah 35:6, the lame becomes an image of hope: "Then the lame will leap like a deer," a promise of messianic restoration. In Jeremiah 31:8, the lame are part of those whom God brings back from the land of the north, a sign of His inclusive mercy.
H6455.portee: The figure of the lame in the Bible teaches the Christian two complementary truths. First, it shows human limitations in the face of the perfection that worship once required: the disabled were kept at a distance, reflecting a theology where Mosaic purity was linked to physical integrity. But the prophecies, especially in Isaiah, overturn this logic by promising that the lame will walk and run in the time of divine fulfillment. It is a powerful image of redemption and healing that God works in Christ, who excludes no one. For the believer, it reminds us that true integrity is not physical, but spiritual, and that God includes the weak.

sens: Statue or object shaped to represent a deity
Religious artwork sculpted or carved
Material representation of a false god
That which diverts the heart from worshiping the true God
H6456.detail:
1. An idol is primarily a statue or image sculpted or carved from stone or wood, intended to represent a god or a deity of pagan worship. It is a material object made by human hands. In Deuteronomy 7:5, God commands Israel to overthrow the altars and break the idols of the nations — these are concrete structures to be destroyed.
2. The term also refers to all religious representations that are carved or sculpted: statues dedicated to worship. In 2 Chronicles 34:4, King Josiah breaks the idols and carved images set up on the altars of false gods — all objects of idolatrous worship to be eliminated.
3. Figuratively, an idol represents any false god, any object of erroneous worship: not only the stone object but the deceptive divine being it claims to embody. Isaiah 42:8 asserts that the Lord will not give His glory to idols — He refuses to share His worship with false gods.
4. More broadly, it is that which diverts the human heart from worshiping the true God and fixes it on a creature or a false deity. Hosea 11:2 reproaches Israel for multiplying idols: it is infidelity, a heart that turns away.
H6456.origine: The Hebrew word פָּסִיל (pe.sil) comes from the root פסל (p-s-l), which means "to carve," "to sculpt," "to shape." An idol is therefore literally something that is carved or shaped, a crafted object. The word carries the image of human effort to create a material representation of a god — which is precisely what the Lord forbids His people. The variant פֶּסֶל (pesèl) is encountered with the same meaning and root.
H6456.emploi: The word pe.sil appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the historical and prophetic books. It is used very consistently: it always designates an object of idolatrous worship that the people of God must reject or destroy. Religious reformers like Josiah (2 Chronicles 34:3-4) target idols to purify worship. The prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah denounce them as powerless and deceptive (Isaiah 10:10; Isaiah 42:8; Jeremiah 50:38). The word can also refer to a quarry or a mine (Judges 3:19), as stone is shaped there — even an image of shaping. At the heart of the Bible, this word reminds us of the radical incompatibility between the worship of the true God and the adoration of materialized false gods.
H6456.portee: This word calls the believer to examine their heart: what receives my worship and service? An idol is not just a stone statue; it is any creature, any wealth, any ambition that takes the place that only God deserves. Understanding what the Bible calls an idol helps to unmask modern false gods that captivate our hearts away from the living God.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher, son of Japhlet
H6457.detail: Pasac is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned only in the genealogy of the sons of Japhlet (1 Chronicles 7:33). He appears alongside his brothers Bimhal and Ashvath, in a genealogical list that traces the descendants of Asher before the Israelite monarchy.
H6457.origine: The name Pasac means "cut off" or "separated" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of separation or division. It comes from a Hebrew root expressing cutting. Like many other proper names in the Old Testament, it carries a meaning that perhaps reflected a circumstance or quality noted at the birth or in the life of the character.
H6457.emploi: Pasac appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:33, where he is presented as the son of Japhlet and brother of Bimhal and Ashvath. He is listed in the genealogies of the descendants of Asher, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. His existence and lineage are not developed elsewhere in the biblical texts; he plays no notable narrative role, and we know of him only this simple genealogical connection.

sens: To work stone or wood by removing material with a tool
To give shape to a rough stone by working it
To prepare the material for construction
H6458.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a concrete manual act: removing chips from stone or wood with a tool (chisel, hammer) to shape the raw material. Moses "carved" two stone tablets for the Ten Commandments (Exodus 34:1, 34:4), which implies precise and regular work.
2. More broadly, it is to give a final and usable shape to a material that does not yet have one. Moses "carved" the tablets "like the first ones" (Deuteronomy 10:3), meaning he reproduced the original shape exactly.
3. In construction, Solomon's workers "carved" the stones and wood to build the temple (1 Kings 5:18): the work of carving prepares the material for its use in the building.
4. Figuratively, the word can refer to one who makes idols: a "worker" who "carves" an image (Habakkuk 2:18), thus shaping an object of worship—revealing the prophet's irony in the face of the lies of false gods.
H6458.origine: The root הסל (psalal) fundamentally means "to cut" or "to slice." It evokes the image of the chisel that removes excess material to reveal the shape hidden in the raw block. The word belongs to the family of action verbs applied to the work of stone and wood, common in the vocabulary of construction in Israel.
H6458.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the Bible, primarily in contexts of sacred or civil construction. The first three occurrences (Exodus 34:1; 34:4; Deuteronomy 10:1, 10:3) concern the making of the tablets of the Law, a foundational act that connects human work to divine action. One occurrence (1 Kings 5:18) describes the work of the artisans of Solomon's temple, showing how carving is a structured professional act. The last occurrence (Habakkuk 2:18) plays on the word critically: the sculptor of idols "carves" his mute gods, highlighting the absurdity of a deity shaped by human hands.
H6458.portee: This word reminds us that manual labor is honorable and sacred: carving the stone of the tablets of the Law is not a trivial act, but a task entrusted by God. It also states that all human creation, even beautiful and crafted, is worthless if it claims to replace the true God—this is the heart of Habakkuk's message against idols.

sens: An object shaped by hand, usually from wood or stone, representing a deity or supernatural being
A visible representation of a god, used for worship
An object of adoration and religious trust
A human creation elevated to the status of a god
H6459.detail:
1. The word primarily designates simply a sculpted, chiseled, or engraved image in material—wood, stone, metal. It is a visible representation, an object that can be touched and seen. Exodus 20:4 formally prohibits it: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image."
2. This carved image is never neutral: it serves the worship of a deity. It is adored, spoken to, and help or protection is expected from it. In Judges 18:17-18, the Danites steal the carved image from a house, the ephod, and the teraphim—this is a religious act, a conquest of sacred objects.
3. The word takes on a critical nuance among the prophets: the carved image becomes the emblem of false religion, misplaced trust. Isaiah 42:17 speaks of those who "trust in carved idols." It promises what cannot hold— a god of wood or stone that has no power to save (Isaiah 45:20).
4. Ultimately, the carved image represents everything a human shapes with their hands and elevates to the status of a god. It is the most carnal religious misunderstanding: to believe that a manufactured object can be a god.
H6459.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to chisel" or "to carve." It is the action of shaping stone or wood that gives its name to the object. In Hebrew, there is also a related form, pesil (with a different vowel), which has the same meaning. The underlying verb evokes the artisan who removes material, chip by chip, to create a shape. The Bible uses this term precisely because it recalls human effort: it is a "handmade" image, not descended from heaven.
H6459.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Law (Exodus, Deuteronomy, Leviticus), among the Prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Nahum, Habakkuk), and in historical narratives (Judges, Kings, Chronicles). In the Law, it appears in formal prohibitions against idol worship, particularly in the Decalogue (Exodus 20:4, Deuteronomy 5:8). In the narratives of Judges (the story of Micah and the Danites), the carved image is a coveted and stolen cult object. The narratives of Kings show unfaithful kings having them made in the Temple itself (2 Kings 21:7). Among the prophets, the term is laden with irony: they extensively describe the making of a carved idol to show its absurdity (Isaiah 44:9-17). The carved image is thus the focal point of the biblical critique of idolatry: it embodies the materiality, falsehood, and powerlessness of worship that does not address the living God.
H6459.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that true worship of the living God stands in radical opposition to any attempt to represent Him by an image or material object. The prohibition of the carved image is not a ritual detail: it protects the heart against the illusion that God can be "captured" or "manipulated" by what our hands create. It is a lesson of faith: placing trust in the invisible Lord, not in visible human creations. It also invites the believer to examine their own hidden idols—everything they elevate in place of God.

sens: stringed musical instrument, triangular in shape
instrument used in the official orchestras of the king of Babylon
H6460.detail:
1. The sambuca is a stringed musical instrument, probably triangular in shape. It is a wind instrument that produces musical sounds by vibrating under the finger or bow. Its Greek name derives from similar instruments known in Asia Minor and Egypt.

2. In the account of Daniel, the sambuca is among the instruments of the royal orchestra of King Nebuchadnezzar, alongside the trumpet, the flute, and the psaltery. It is played during the ceremony where all peoples must bow down before the golden statue (Daniel 3:5,7,10,15). It thus represents an instrument of power and solemnity, used to mark the commands of the king and impose his authority.
H6460.origine: The Greek word "psalterion" (ψαλτήριον) borrows from the Semitic root meaning "to pluck" or "to make the strings vibrate." The term "sambuca" is the Greek transcription of an eastern instrument renowned in antiquity. It belongs to the family of plucked string instruments, like the harp or lyre.
H6460.emploi: This word appears only four times in the entire Bible, concentrated in chapter 3 of Daniel (verses 5, 7, 10, 15). Each occurrence describes the same moment: the ceremony of King Nebuchadnezzar ordering all the peoples of his empire to bow down before his golden statue. The sambuca is always associated with other musical instruments, appearing in the official list of the Babylonian royal orchestra. The context suggests a prestigious and imposing instrument, worthy of eastern royal courts.
H6460.portee: For the Christian reader, the sambuca reminds us that human power, even the most lavish with its orchestras and statues, cannot impose faith. It is through this noise of music that Nebuchadnezzar commands idolatry, but God will protect those who refuse to bow down. This instrument thus becomes a symbol of the seduction and pressure of the world, against which the believer must remain faithful.

sens: To fade away, cease to be visible or present
To cease to exist, vanish
To lack, be missing
H6461.detail:
1. Disappear means to fade away, no longer being present. The psalmist says that the godly men "disappear" among other men (Psalms 12:2): they vanish from sight, they are no longer seen, they are no longer noticed.
2. The word also evokes the idea of ceasing, of going away. In Psalms 12:2, we see the faithful going away and disappearing, as if a generation were to extinguish.
3. By extension, disappear can mean that something is lacking or missing: what should be there is no longer present.
H6461.origine: The Hebrew root describes the idea of going away, gradually fading. The word expresses the movement from the visible to the invisible, like something that dissolves or moves away until it is no longer perceived. It is a simple and concrete verb, with few derivatives in Hebrew.
H6461.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 12:2. The psalmist describes the disappearance of faithful and godly men: in a world where dishonesty reigns, the good men go away, cease to be noticed. This context shows that the word speaks not only of a physical disappearance but of the social and spiritual erasure of those who remain righteous.
H6461.portee: This word reminds us that faithfulness may seem to fade in the face of lies and injustice. The psalmist sees the righteous disappear, overwhelmed by dishonesty: it is a cry of distress in the face of this apparent silence of the godly. It invites us not to abandon justice, even if it seems to vanish from the world.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher during the divided monarchy
H6462.detail: Pispa is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the Bible. He was the son of Jether and the brother of Jephunné and Ara, all three belonging to the tribe of Asher. His name appears in the genealogy of Asher, which lists the descendants of this patriarch at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two kingdoms (Israel and Judah).
H6462.origine: The name Pispa literally means "disappearance." It is a typical Hebrew name from the genealogies of Israel, formed according to the onomastic conventions of ancient times.
H6462.emploi: Pispa is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:38, in the context of a genealogy of the sons of Jether from the tribe of Asher. The genealogies in the book of Chronicles list the descendants of the twelve tribes of Israel, and Pispa appears simply as one of the three sons of Jether, with no other historical or narrative detail.

sens: To utter cries of distress or suffering
To express pain through guttural and convulsive sounds
To manifest intense anguish or agony
H6463.detail:
1. The word designates the cry that escapes from a person in the grip of extreme suffering — an involuntary, visceral cry that cannot be held back. Isaiah 42:14 uses it to describe the cries of a woman in labor: it is the peak of physical pain.

2. This cry is not an articulated word, but a manifestation of the tortured body: groans, gasps, shouts that express what cannot be said otherwise. The image evokes a wounded creature or a childbirth where suffering becomes noise.

3. The verb also carries the idea of an inner agitation that cannot remain contained — the pain or anguish must escape, no matter the cost, or it suffocates the one who bears it.
H6463.origine: The Hebrew root פָּעָה expresses the action of crying out, probably imitating the sound itself. It is rare in the Bible and concentrated on the expression of the most acute distress — that where ordered words disappear to leave only the cry of the body.
H6463.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 42:14. The prophet describes the moment when God, after a long silence, will finally act to save His people. This action is compared to that of a woman in labor who can no longer hold back her cries: she "will cry out," says the text. This indicates that God's silence is not passivity, but a restrained force, and that His intervention will be as irresistible and vital as the cries of childbirth.
H6463.portee: This word reminds the believer that suffering has the right to be expressed — even before God. The psalms make use of it when they confess distress. Isaiah 42 also suggests that God hears these cries and is not insensitive: God's silence is never indifference, but an expectation filled with intention. For the reader, it is an invitation not to stifle their pain, but to bring it before God without guilt.

sens: Capital of King Hadar of Edom
H6464.detail: 1. Pau is a city that served as the capital of King Hadar (also called Hadad), one of the last kings of Edom. The Bible mentions it twice when listing the kings of Edom and their royal cities: once in Genesis 36:39 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:50, where it is spelled slightly differently ("Pahi"). The name itself could mean "bleating," recalling the pastoral farming typical of the region of Edom, but the exact location has not been definitively identified by archaeologists.
H6464.origine: The Hebrew name פָּעוּ (pa'ou) evokes the sound of the bleating of goats and sheep (the onomatopoeia "pahi"), suggesting a region of pastures and livestock. This etymology reflects the pastoral character of the region of Edom, populated by shepherds and herders. The name reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:50 with the variant "Pahi," likely an alternative transcription of the same Hebrew toponym.
H6464.emploi: Pau appears only twice in the Bible, both in genealogical lists of the kings of Edom. In Genesis 36:39, it is mentioned as the city of King Hadar after Baal-Hanan has gone. The same passage is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:50 with the historical parallel, where the king and his wife are named again. These two occurrences are copies of the same genealogical tradition, likely written to establish and memorize the succession of Edomite kings and their centers of power.

sens: Mountain peak in Moab in the Abarim range, near Pisgah
H6465.detail: Peor is a mountain peak located in Moab, in the Abarim mountain range, near Pisgah. It is there that Balak brought the prophet Balaam to curse Israel (Numbers 23:28). The place is especially famous for the apostasy that occurred there: the Israelites engaged in idolatry by worshiping the gods of Moab, seduced by Moabite women (Numbers 25:18 and 31:16). This "affair of Peor" was a grave sin that brought a plague upon the people (Joshua 22:17).
H6465.origine: The name literally means "gap" or "cleft," which well describes the appearance of a ridge or rocky peak. It is a simple Hebrew name that directly designates the geography of the place.
H6465.emploi: Peor appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate this place in Moab. Three occurrences speak of the "affair of Peor" (Numbers 25 and 31, Joshua 22), a serious event where Israel committed idolatry and sexual immorality with the Moabites, which provoked a divine plague. One occurrence (Numbers 23) mentions the peak itself, where Balaam was brought to curse Israel. The name thus carries negative resonances: it recalls both a religious temptation and divine discipline.
H6465.portee: The affair of Peor shows how serious idolatry and religious compromise are in the eyes of the Lord, and how they attract His judgment. For the Christian reader, this account invites vigilance against the seductions of the world and the compromises that distance one from God, even within the people of God.

sens: to accomplish an action, to realize something
to create, to build, to manufacture
to commit a blameworthy act or a sin
to act, to conduct oneself in a certain way
H6466.detail:
1. To accomplish an action, to realize something: this is the most general meaning. The verb refers to any action that one undertakes and successfully completes. In Exodus 15:17, God "has founded" the sanctuary, meaning He constructed and established it with His own hands.
2. To create, to build, to manufacture: the verb takes on a nuance of creation or production. In Isaiah 44:12, the craftsman "works the iron" with a hammer to make an object. It is the action of transforming material according to a plan.
3. To commit a blameworthy act or a sin: the verb is used to describe evil actions, especially transgressions of God's law. In Psalms 119:3, it is said of those who love the law that they "do not commit iniquity." The word then emphasizes the moral responsibility of the one who acts wrongly.
4. To act, to conduct oneself in a certain way: this refers to the general conduct of a person. In Psalms 11:3, when the foundations are shaken, "what would" the righteous do? — the verb questions their ability to act righteously in a crisis.
H6466.origine: The Hebrew root פעל (paal) means "to do, to act." It is close to the notion of work and concrete action. The word can also refer to the worker or one who acts (פעיל, poêl), the one who accomplishes the action. This root belongs to a family of terms expressing activity and production, and it is very common in biblical Hebrew to describe both divine action and human action.
H6466.emploi: The verb "to do" is used 56 times in the Hebrew Bible in the provided references. It appears mainly in the Psalms, the book of Job, and the prophets. Its meaning varies according to the context: it can refer to the works of God (Exodus 15:17, Psalms 74:12), the activity of craftsmen (Isaiah 44:12 and following), or human acts, particularly evil acts (Job 34:22, Psalms 59:3, Isaiah 31:2). In contexts of justice, the word often takes on a moral hue: one "commits" iniquity (Psalms 119:3), one "acts" badly or well. The verb thus serves as the instrument through which the Bible speaks of responsibility: we are what we do.
H6466.portee: This verb reminds that the Christian life is measured by actions: faith without works is dead. It invites the believer to be aware that their actions, big or small, are the fruit of their moral choices and that God sees them. But it also comforts by showing that God acts justly in history and accomplishes His sovereign plans, while the works of the unjust will ultimately collapse.

sens: Action of doing, activity
Result of an action, creation
Paid work, salary
Reward deserved by actions
Acquisition, what one obtains through effort
H6467.detail:
1. The work primarily refers to the action itself, the act of doing or working: it is the ongoing activity. Job speaks of the worker who "goes out in the morning" to seek food (Job 24:5) — it is the daily work, the work of the day.
2. It is also the concrete result of this action: what is done, created, completed. God contemplates His works and finds them perfect (Deuteronomy 32:4) — it refers to all that God has created and accomplished.
3. The word also refers to the remuneration attached to work, the earned salary. When it says "render to them according to their works" (Psalms 28:4), it speaks of the reward or punishment one deserves for their actions.
4. By extension, a work can be an acquisition, a treasure obtained through effort or ingenuity — like the treasures "acquired" by a deceitful tongue (Proverbs 21:6), which are quickly lost.
5. In biblical thought, the work reveals character: one knows someone by their works, as they express what they truly are (Proverbs 20:11).
H6467.origine: The Hebrew word פֹּעַל comes from a root that expresses the idea of doing, acting, working. It primarily designates the action, then naturally its fruit. It is a very common word in the Bible, especially in the Psalms and in biblical wisdom (Job, Proverbs), where it allows for discussion of what man or God accomplishes. It stands in contrast to vain words: a work is something real, concrete.
H6467.emploi: The word appears 37 times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and Job. The usages show that the Lord "observes" the works of men and rewards them (Job 34:11: "He renders to each according to their works"). Men are judged by their works — those of the wicked condemn them (Psalms 28:4), while those of the righteous testify to their character (Proverbs 20:11). In the prophets, the works of the Lord are acts of salvation or judgment that one must "see" and meditate on (Isaiah 5:12, Habakkuk 1:5). The word can also simply refer to daily work, the task one accomplishes (Job 24:5).
H6467.portee: This word reminds the believer that their actions carry weight — they reveal what they are, and God sees and judges them justly. It invites us to contemplate the works of the Lord to nourish our faith: His creations and interventions are the mirror of His wisdom and faithfulness. It is also an exhortation to vigilance: our works define us; they do not deceive the One who scrutinizes hearts.

sens: The payment owed for the work of a laborer or day laborer
The concrete result of an action or work
The consequence or reward that someone receives in return for their behavior or actions
H6468.detail:
1. The wage is primarily the payment owed to the one who has worked: it is the money, the gain that the worker deserves for their days of labor. In Leviticus 19:13, God forbids the employer of a hired worker from withholding their wage until the next day — they must be paid without delay, as it is a debt of justice.

2. The word also designates the work itself, the concrete fruit of an action. In Psalms 17:4, the psalmist stands guard "against the way of the violent" by observing their actions; here the word depicts the work, the acts one performs that can be either bad or good.

3. By extension, wage becomes the moral or divine consequence that follows our actions: what one receives in return, whether deserved or not. The wicked "makes a deceitful gain" in Proverbs 11:18, while the righteous "has a true wage" — God Himself rewards actions. In Isaiah 62:11, the rewards go before the Lord, showing that God brings with Him the just consequence of our works.
H6468.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to do, to accomplish": a pelu llah is thus literally the fruit of doing, the accomplishment of an action. This image of work producing a concrete result naturally extends to reward — the product of work belongs to the one who accomplished it. The Hebrew word was used in all contexts where one spoke of what one receives in exchange: from the wages of workers to the divine consequences of human actions.
H6468.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah. It primarily designates the concrete wage of the worker (Leviticus 19:13) or the hired hand, but quickly extends to a figurative sense. In the Psalms (17:4, 28:5, 109:20), it becomes the moral retribution — God rewards or punishes according to actions. The prophets use it to announce the consequences of the people's conduct (Isaiah 49:4, 62:11, 65:7): the righteous receives their reward, the wicked their punishment. Jeremiah (31:16) and Ezekiel (29:20) use the word in this eschatological sense: the work accomplished in service to God will have its reward.
H6468.portee: This word reminds the believer of a fundamental truth: work has value, and God does not leave without reward the one who acts justly. It also encourages moral vigilance — our actions produce fruits, visible or not immediately, but real. For the one who suffers in serving God, like Isaiah, the word promises that their reward will come, that this work is not in vain. It is a promise of divine justice: God sees and pays what is just.

sens: Man of the tribe of Levi, son of Obed-Edom
Porter of the temple during the united monarchy of Israel
H6469.detail: Peulthaï is a Levite, son of Obed-Edom, who lived during the time of the united monarchy of Israel. He was the eighth son of his family and served as a porter of the temple, responsible for guarding one of the gates of the house of God. His name, which means "God has made," reflects the importance of his family in divine service.
H6469.origine: The name Peulthaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "work" or "deed" (from the root paal, "to act" or "to do"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it evokes the action of God in the life of the name bearer. Several of his brothers also bear Levitical names: Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sachar, Nethanel, Issachar, and Ammiel.
H6469.emploi: Peulthaï is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 26:5. He appears in the list of the sons of Obed-Edom, a respected Levite who had received a special blessing from God. This mention highlights his role in the organization of worship and the guarding of the temple during the time of King David. The text specifies that he was "the eighth" son and that God had blessed his family, thus recognizing their faithfulness in divine service.
H6469.portee: This character illustrates the importance of Levitical families in the service of the temple and of God in Israel. His existence and that of his brothers remind us that worship relied on entire families devoted to guarding and maintaining the house of God. It is an example of a calling passed down through a lineage and of divine blessing on those who dedicate themselves to the service of God.

sens: To push, shake physically
To disturb the mind, to deeply worry
To be troubled, to be agitated
H6470.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to push, shake, hit repeatedly, as one would shake something to set it in motion. It is the action of giving blows or repeated impulses.
2. Figuratively, the word denotes the disturbance of the mind, the deep anxiety that fills a person. When Pharaoh has dreams, his mind is "agitated" (Genesis 41:8): he cannot find peace, he desperately seeks the answer. It is also the Spirit of the Lord that "agitates" Samson, giving him an inner strength and push to fulfill his mission (Judges 13:25).
3. To be troubled means to experience an inner disturbance that paralyzes or activates: the psalmist in his trouble cannot speak (Psalms 77:5), while Nebuchadnezzar cannot sleep, consumed by worry (Daniel 2:1).
H6470.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses impulse, repeated and vigorous movement. The basic image is that of a blow, a jolt, that sets something in motion. The word retains this dual meaning: first physical (to shake, to push), then transferred to the life of the soul and spirit (to disturb, to deeply worry).
H6470.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. It describes either the disturbance of a man's mind (Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar troubled by their inexplicable dreams), or an inner anxiety preventing rest, or the action of the Spirit of God pushing a man to act (Samson). In all cases, the word expresses a disturbance that shakes the interior of a person, whether anxious or driven to action.
H6470.portee: This word reminds us that the anxiety of the mind can paralyze, but also that a divine force can stir the heart of a believer to push him to fulfill his mission. For the modern reader, it helps to recognize those moments when one feels shaken from within, either by anxiety or by God's call to act.

sens: Distinct moment, occasion when something occurs
Number of repetitions of an action or event
Foot or step, the means of moving
Blow or strike, violent or repeated gesture
H6471.detail:
1. A "time" is a particular moment or occasion: it is the instant when something happens. When Adam says of the woman, "This time is bone of my bones," he speaks of that precise moment when she is presented to him (Genesis 2:23). The word thus designates the singular occasion, the moment as an event.

2. The word also indicates the number of repetitions: "how many times" or "so many times." When Elijah tells his servant, "Go back" seven times, he repeats the action seven successive occasions (1 Kings 18:43). Or again: "You have insulted me ten times," meaning ten occurrences of the insult (Job 19:3).

3. Foot or step is its primary, concrete meaning. The word designates the foot of a man or the hoof of an animal. This less frequent usage in French translates the basic image: the trace of the step, the contact of the foot with the ground.

4. A blow or a strike: the word also evokes the repeated action of striking. When Samson asks God, "Give me strength just this time, and let me take vengeance in one blow," he speaks of a unique but violent action (Judges 16:28). The verb "to strike" or "to seek" is even used with this word when enumerating: "so many times you have done this to me."
H6471.origine: The Hebrew word פַּעַם (pa'am) comes from a root that first evokes the idea of walking or taking a step, then the contact of the foot with the ground—the dull sound of the step. From there derives the image of a blow, a repeated strike, and finally the occasion, the time when it occurs. The word thus designates both the moment of an action and its number: once, ten times. It is a very common word in the Bible, particularly when it is necessary to count or enumerate occasions.
H6471.emploi: The word פַּעַם appears 108 times in the Hebrew Bible and largely means "time" or "occasion." It is especially found in Genesis and Exodus to enumerate: "three times a year" you shall appear before the Lord (Exodus 34:24), "ten times" you have insulted me (Job 19:3). Often it is accompanied by a number: "once," "twice," "seven times." The word also appears to mark uniqueness: "this time" or "this time around" emphasizes that it is the present moment, now. Sometimes it retains its meaning of foot or blow (for example in Exodus 25:12, the feet of the ark). The context changes the nuance: in a prayer, one counts the times one has failed; in a procession, one enumerates the turns.
H6471.portee: For the reader, this simple word reveals how God counts every moment, every occasion. When the Bible enumerates "seven times," "ten times," it shows both repetition and the weight of each instant. Understanding that "time" comes from the step of the foot helps grasp the biblical idea of the path, of walking in the presence of God: we move step by step, moment by moment. It is a word of everyday life that anchors faith in the concrete.

sens: small sound-producing metal object attached to a garment to produce sound when moving
ornament hanging from the high priest's robe
H6472.detail:
1. A bell is a small hollow metal object that jingles when shaken. In the Bible, they adorned the robe of the high priest: "You shall put on its hem, at the bottom, pomegranates of blue, purple, and scarlet, intertwined with bells of gold" (Exodus 28:33). These small golden bells were alternated with pomegranates all around the bottom of the garment.
2. These bells had a specific function during the service in the sanctuary. Their sound announced the movements of the high priest when he entered or exited the holy place: "a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, on all the hem of the robe, for service" (Exodus 39:26). They served to signal his presence and sacred activity.
H6472.origine: The Hebrew word פַּעֲמֹן (pa'amon) comes from the root פַּעַם (pa'am) which means "blow," "step," "time" — the idea of repeated sound and movement. The name literally designates what resounds with each step or gesture. It is a specifically Hebrew word, particular to the vocabulary of Israelite worship.
H6472.emploi: The word appears only four times in the Bible, all in Exodus, and all to describe the bells of the high priest's robe during the making of his sacred garments (Exodus 28:33-34 and 39:25-26). The first two passages give the divine order to Moses; the next two report its execution. It is a highly specialized term in the vocabulary of the sanctuary, with no figurative use.
H6472.portee: These bells remind us that divine worship involves the attention of the whole being: the senses also participate in communion with God. The regular sound of the bells, audible even outside the holy place, signified that the high priest was faithfully fulfilling his role as intercessor before God for the people. It is a lesson in the visibility and audibility of sacred service.

sens: Open the mouth, the jaws wide open
Emit a word, a cry, a sigh by opening the mouth
Devour, engulf by widely opening the mouth
Prepare to receive or welcome eagerly
H6473.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to open the mouth or jaws very wide. In Job 16:10, Job's enemies "open" their mouths to devour him, striking him — it is an image of threat and hostility, like a beast preparing to bite.
2. The word also describes the act of speaking, letting out a sound from one's mouth. In Psalms 119:131, the psalmist "opens" his mouth and sighs: he expresses his intense desire for God's commandments through this simple and moving gesture.
3. When the mouth opens without limit, it can engulf or devour. In Isaiah 5:14, the grave "opens" its mouth and "widens" its jaws to receive the rich and the noisy of Zion — an image of the insatiable abyss that swallows everything.
4. Finally, "open the mouth" can express expectation, the readiness to receive. In Job 29:23, people "opened" their mouths as for a spring rain — they turned to him with hope, waiting for his life-giving words.
H6473.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּעַר comes from a root that evokes yawning, spreading, and opening. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "to widen" or "to part." The basic image is that of a mouth opening wide, of spacing or a fissure. It is a concrete and vivid word, very alive in biblical poetry.
H6473.emploi: This verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always with the mouth as the subject or complement, and always to evoke something dramatic or intense. In Job 16:10, the mouth that opens is that of an enemy attacking. In Job 29:23, it expresses expectation and trust. In Psalms 119:131, it manifests desire and supplication. In Isaiah 5:14, it represents the jaws of Sheol, insatiable and devouring. Each time, the verb creates a striking image: opening the mouth is an act that reveals an emotion or intention — hostile, hopeful, desirous, or deadly.
H6473.portee: This word reminds us that speech always begins with an opening: we must open our mouths to speak, pray, cry out to God. It is also an image of vulnerability — the open mouth exposes. Finally, "open the mouth" suggests eagerness and intensity: when we are hungry, we open wide; when we plead, we open wide. It invites us to examine ourselves: with what desire, what intention do we open our mouths?

sens: warrior from Elephantine (or the Arabian desert) in the service of King David
H6474.detail: Paaraï is a proper name that designates a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 23:35. He is part of the list of David's renowned warriors, those who fought alongside him and helped him conquer and consolidate his kingdom. His nickname, "the Arab," likely indicates that he came from a desert or mountainous region — either Elephantine (a mountainous area in Judea) or an Arab region — making him a local warrior, enduring and experienced.
H6474.origine: The name Paaraï comes from a root that means "to yawn," that is, "to open the mouth" or "to open wide" — hence the literal meaning "the one who yawns" or "the one who opens." It is a concrete and vivid name, like many ancient Hebrew names, which perhaps evoked a quality of the warrior or a forgotten anecdote.
H6474.emploi: Paaraï appears only once in Scripture: in 2 Samuel 23:35, in the list of David's "mighty men." This list, also called "the Thirty" or "the Thirty-Seven," gathers the bravest warriors who followed David during the conquest wars and played a decisive role in establishing his kingdom. Paaraï is identified as "the Arab," which situates him geographically and socially among the warriors from the peripheral regions of the kingdom. No account tells us his exploits in detail — the Bible merely names him, which attests to the importance of these men's roles in official history.

sens: Open the mouth to speak
Open wide the mouth to strike or devour
Let loose, utter
Deliver from danger, save
Manifest, act openly
H6475.detail:
1. To open the mouth to speak or express something: this is the act of taking the floor. In Ezekiel 2:8, the prophet is invited to "open his mouth" to receive the words of God, meaning to listen and welcome His message.
2. To open wide the mouth as a weapon or a gesture of threat: enemies "open" their mouths against the psalmist (Psalms 22:14), like a lion preparing to devour. This is an act of aggression.
3. To let loose a promise or vow by uttering it: in Judges 11:36, Jephthah "opened his mouth" by making a vow to the Lord—his word came out of his lips and cannot be taken back.
4. To deliver someone from danger or to save: in a figurative sense, "open" means to liberate, to snatch from peril. In Psalms 144:7, the psalmist asks God to "deliver" him from the furious waters and the hands of foreigners.
5. The earth itself can "open" its mouth as an active power: in Deuteronomy 11:6 and Numbers 16:30, the earth opens to swallow the rebels, thus manifesting divine judgment.
H6475.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the primary idea of "to part," "to open," "to separate." The basic image is that of something opening or dividing—a mouth that opens, the earth that splits. The related noun "petsah" refers to a wound or a breach. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb is rendered by forms of "anoigô" (to open), which carries the same concrete idea: to create an opening or access.
H6475.emploi: This verb appears fifteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and in narrative or prophetic texts. It is first used in a concrete sense: to open the mouth to speak (Ezekiel 2:8), or for the earth to open in judgment (Numbers 16:30, Deuteronomy 11:6). It also describes the hostile act of opening the mouth or jaws against someone (Psalms 22:14, Lamentations 2:16). In parallel, it takes on a more figurative sense of "deliverance" or "liberation" (Psalms 144:7, 144:11), and it expresses the idea of making a vow solemnly (Judges 11:35-36: "to open the mouth" to make a vow means to pronounce it publicly and commit to it). The context determines whether the gesture is one of creating speech, aggression, or salvation.
H6475.portee: This verb reminds us of the power of words: to open one's mouth is to act, to create or destroy through speech. For the believer, it evokes the importance of what we say and the God who listens. It also emphasizes that deliverance comes from God: He is the one who "opens" the prophet's mouth to entrust him with His message, and He is the one who delivers those who cry out to Him. Finally, it shows that vows made to God are not empty words: once the mouth is "opened" to pronounce them, they bind the one who makes them.

sens: Burst suddenly with force and noise
Resound intensely (a cry, an exclamation)
Manifest exuberantly one's joy
H6476.detail: 1. The word first describes a physical phenomenon: something that breaks and bursts forth suddenly, like a dam giving way. In Isaiah 55:12, "the trees of the field will burst into applause," the image is one of an explosion of joy that spreads. 2. It means to sound out loudly, particularly a voice or a cry. Isaiah 44:23 calls the mountains to "burst into cries of joy"—this is to make one's voice heard with force, as if the mountain itself were crying out. 3. In almost all usages, the word expresses joy that cannot be contained: it must come out, overflow, explode. Isaiah 54:1 tells the barren woman to "burst forth" in her joy—this invites a demonstration of exuberant and joyful deliverance received.
H6476.origine: The Hebrew root evokes breaking, bursting: something that breaks and suddenly bursts forth. The verb pitsah belongs to the family of words describing abrupt breaks or eruptions. The image is concrete and dynamic: a violent and sudden movement that disrupts a balance.
H6476.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the prophecies of Isaiah (6 occurrences). It is never neutral: it always accompanies the idea of deliverance, restoration, redemption. Psalms 98:4 invites the inhabitants of the earth to burst forth in joy before the Lord who has performed wonders. Isaiah 14:7 (after the fall of Babylon), 44:23 and 49:13 (announcing the comfort of Israel), 52:9 (to restored Jerusalem), 54:1 (to the barren woman who has become a mother)—it is always the overflowing joy of salvation regained. The word never denotes a tranquil joy, but the irrepressible explosion of joy in the face of God's wonders.
H6476.portee: This verb reminds the believer that authentic joy in the face of God's salvation must not remain silent or contained. It is meant to burst forth, to manifest publicly, to make one's voice resound. It is an invitation not to stifle thanksgiving but to let it spring forth unreservedly—through cries, songs, visible manifestations of gratitude. For the Christian, it is a reminder that the redemption obtained in Jesus Christ deserves a reaction that is anything but indifferent or murmured.

sens: The cutting edge of a tool or weapon
The state of wear of a blade or tool that loses its effectiveness
H6477.detail:
1. The edge is the cutting edge of a tool, which makes it capable of cutting or plowing. In 1 Samuel 13:21, it speaks of the "edge of the plowshares, the mattocks, the forks, and the axes": this is the part of these agricultural tools that penetrates the earth and does the work.
2. The word also designates the state of this edge: when the edge is good, the tool works well; when it is "dull," the tool no longer cuts and becomes useless. In the same verse, the text recounts that the Philistines prevented the Israelites from sharpening their tools: without an edge, it is impossible to plow or fight.
H6477.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that speaks of the action of cutting, slicing, or pressing. It is a concrete term that primarily describes the physical aspect of a tool: its edge, its ability to cut. The family of Hebrew words encompasses the idea of an action applied with force or sharpness.
H6477.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 13:21. This passage describes a military strategy of the Philistines: they forbade the Israelites from having a blacksmith to sharpen their tools and weapons. Without an edge—meaning without effective tools or sharp weapons—the Israelites were disarmed, both for agricultural work and for war. The context shows that the edge was a sign of freedom, of the ability to work and defend oneself.
H6477.portee: This passage teaches that tools for work and defense are a vital necessity for a free people. It is a lesson on the importance of preparation, equipment, and autonomy: a people without sharp tools is a people enslaved and weakened.

sens: remove the bark from a branch or wood
expose the white surface of a plant
reveal what was hidden under an outer layer
H6478.detail: 1. To peel means to remove the bark from a branch or trunk. It is a material, physical gesture: one scrapes or removes the outer layer of wood to reveal what is underneath. In Genesis 30:37, Jacob peels branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees to expose the white wood. 2. The verb evokes the idea of exposing, making visible the white surface hidden under the brown bark. Once the bark is removed, the contrast between the light wood and the dark bark becomes visible. Jacob does this deliberately to show this white to the animals. 3. Figuratively, to peel represents the action of revealing, exposing what was concealed or covered. The gesture performed on the wood symbolizes a disclosure.
H6478.origine: The Hebrew verb patzal (פָּצַל) literally means "to split" or "to flake" and comes from a root that evokes the idea of breaking or dividing a surface. The word belongs to the family of verbs indicating physical actions on solid materials. In the Piel form (intensive form), patzal reinforces the idea of methodically removing layer by layer.
H6478.emploi: This verb appears twice in the Bible, only in Genesis 30:37-38, in the account where Jacob uses a stratagem to increase his flock of sheep. Jacob peels the branches and places them before the sheep that come to drink, counting on the sight of the white bands to influence their reproductive behavior. The use of the verb is concrete and technical: it describes a precise gesture, without spiritual nuance, in the context of an ancient breeding tactic.
H6478.portee: This passage shows how Jacob uses practical knowledge and observation to achieve his goals. The act of peeling also symbolizes how hidden realities can be revealed through human action. For the Christian reader, this reminds us that God can use ingenuity and natural means to accomplish His purposes, even when the methods employed are human tactics.

sens: Stripe or line drawn on a surface
Peeled or exposed part on a branch
Zone of contrasting color obtained by removing the bark
H6479.detail:
1. A band is a stripe, a line that stands out on a surface — here, on wood. It is an elongated and well-defined mark.
2. More specifically, it is a part of the bark that has been removed, thus exposing the white wood. In Genesis 30:37, Jacob peels branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees to create these visible white bands.
3. The effect obtained is an alternation of colors: the dark bark and the exposed light wood form contrasting bands that mark the branch. This contrast was intentional in the context of the narrative where Jacob places them before the flocks.
H6479.origine: The Hebrew word pétsalah comes from a root that evokes the idea of dividing, separating by distinct marks. It literally designates a visible separation, a demarcation on a surface. The biblical context shows that it is a stripe obtained by peeling or removing a superficial part of an object.
H6479.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 30:37. It is there that Jacob peels branches to create visible white bands. The word precisely describes the visible result of this action: the white stripes of the exposed wood alternating with the remaining bark. The use is concrete and descriptive, without figurative extension.
H6479.portee: This account shows how Jacob, in all simplicity, observes nature and uses visible signs to influence the behavior of animals. This humble attention to the practical details of daily life reminds us that practical wisdom and thoughtful observation of the created world have their place in faith.

sens: Open or split something by breaking it
Create a crack, a breach in a surface
Figuratively, cause a rupture or separation
H6480.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to open or split something by breaking it — as one tears a fabric or surface by forcing it. In Psalms 60:4, God has torn the earth, meaning He has fissured it, split it by His powerful interventions: "You have shaken the earth, you have torn it." 
2. The image evokes breaches, faults that appear: the text immediately speaks of "breaches" that need to be repaired, showing that the word designates the appearance of visible and tangible fissures. 
3. Figuratively, the word expresses a rupture or separation imposed by force — here, the destructive action of God on the earth as a sign of judgment or trial.
H6480.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּצַם (patsam) comes from a primitive root expressing the action of breaking or shattering. It belongs to the family of verbs indicating violent or sudden actions that open, tear, or fragment. The root evokes the concrete image of something breaking under force.
H6480.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 60:4. It is used in a context of divine judgment: the psalmist describes how God has shaken the earth and torn it, causing breaches that make it stagger. The usage is clearly metaphorical, applied to the earth as creation, to express a powerful and destructive intervention of God. The context of the Psalm suggests a national trial, and the verb intensifies the image of judgment by the idea of a deep rupture of the very ground.
H6480.portee: This word reminds us of God's sovereignty over His creation and His ability to shake even the foundations of the world. For the believer, it expresses both the reality of divine judgment and the call to repair and renewal: after the rupture comes restoration, symbolized by the repair of the breaches. It is an invitation to recognize God's action, even in trial.

sens: Strike someone in a way that causes an injury
Cause physical or emotional suffering
H6481.detail:
1. This verb describes the action of striking or hitting violently until causing harm, especially by a crushing blow or repeated strikes. In 1 Kings 20:37, a man says, "Strike me, please!" and the other indeed wounds him with this blow. It is a visible injury that marks the body.
2. More broadly, the word can also refer to the damage or suffering caused by this violence. In the Song of Solomon 5:7, the city guards "strike" and "wound" the one who seeks her beloved: these are repeated blows that cause her to suffer. The word can evoke both the blow and its painful effect.
H6481.origine: This Hebrew verb comes from a root that means "to crush" or "to strike by crushing." The starting image is that of a blow that crushes or grinds. The form used here is the simple form (Qal), which describes the action in its most direct reality: someone strikes and wounds. It is a very concrete word, attached to the idea of physical damage.
H6481.emploi: The verb "wound" appears three times in the Hebrew Bible with this meaning. It is first used to describe injuries caused by blows — as in 1 Kings 20:37 where a prophet orders someone to strike him, and the latter wounds him. It also appears in a scene of urban violence (Song of Solomon 5:7) where the young woman is wounded by the guards. The word can also specifically designate a lesion or crushing (Deuteronomy 23:1), but it always remains linked to the idea of a violent physical injury.
H6481.portee: This word reminds us that violence leaves visible and lasting marks. For the Christian reader, it emphasizes how blows, hurtful words, and persecutions have real consequences — which invites gentleness and respect for the body of others, as Paul teaches when he speaks of the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit.

sens: physical injury to the body, wound or bruise
blow, trauma
moral pain, affliction
mark of devotion or friendship
consequence of sin or evil
H6482.detail:
1. Wound refers to a visible injury to the body: an open wound or a bruise (Exodus 21:25 demands "wound for wound," meaning a compensation equal to the bodily harm inflicted).
2. By extension, the word describes the blows received, traces of violence or shock (Job 9:17: "He who multiplies my wounds without cause").
3. Wound takes on a figurative meaning: it becomes a pain of the heart, a moral affliction (Proverbs 23:29 lists disputes and complaints that lead to "wounds without cause").
4. Curiously, a wound can also express proof of sincere friendship: "The wounds of a friend prove his faithfulness" (Proverbs 27:6), as correction from a true friend is a sign of love.
5. From the biblical perspective of sin, wounds symbolize the consequences of evil: they discipline the wicked and remind of divine retribution (Proverbs 20:30).
H6482.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּצַע comes from a root meaning "to strike" or "to wound." It primarily describes the action of causing a wound, then the mark itself. The word is used for any harm to the body: wound, blow, battle injury, or punishment. It also appears in figurative contexts where the wound symbolizes moral pain or spiritual affliction.
H6482.emploi: The word פֶּצַע (wound) appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Proverbs and the wisdom books. It first denotes a physical reality: a wound or a blow (Exodus 21:25, in the law of retaliation). In Job (9:17), it represents divine affliction. Proverbs uses it to speak of moral correction (20:30), disputes causing harm (23:29), and poignantly to evoke the correction of a faithful friend, which is a form of beneficial wound (27:6). The word thus combines the concrete meaning of physical wound and the figurative sense of suffering or moral affliction that produces good.
H6482.portee: This word teaches that true friendship can involve correction, even when difficult to receive: the wounds of a friend (his rebukes, his discipline) testify to his genuine attachment. It also invites us to see the afflictions of life as opportunities for correction and spiritual growth, not merely as misfortunes, but as tools for transformation for those who receive them wisely.

sens: priest responsible for the temple service during the time of David
H6483.detail: Happitsets is a priest who led one of the rotating divisions of service at the temple during the reign of David. He was the head of the eighteenth division (or course) of priests, which meant that he and the priests of his group were responsible for all the ritual services of the temple during a fixed period of the year (1 Chronicles 24:15). This organization allowed all the priests to fulfill their function in turn, ensuring a constant presence in the service of God.
H6483.origine: The name Happitsets likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to break" or "to fracture." Although the exact meaning and etymology of the name are ancient and poorly documented, it belongs to the tradition of Hebrew names that evoke an action or a divine quality. The name appears only in the lists of priestly organization in 1 Chronicles.
H6483.emploi: Happitsets is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:15, in the list of the heads of the twenty-four divisions of priests established by David for the service of the temple. He appears between Hezir (seventeenth) and another priest in this official enumeration. This list shows how David systematically organized temple worship and the rotation of responsibilities among the priestly families.
H6483.portee: This passage reminds the reader that temple worship relied on a rigorous organization and that each priest had a specific place in the service of God. Even though Happitsets is known to us only by name in an administrative list, he symbolizes those faithful servants of the temple whose dedication, though forgotten by history, was accountable before God.

sens: Exert physical pressure on someone or something
Insist to someone, asking them forcefully and persistently
Bother, harass someone with violence or agitation
Show arrogance, insolence, or presumption
H6484.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is the action of pushing or applying pressure: Lot presses his guests to enter his home in Genesis 19:3, firmly urging them to accept his hospitality. It is a physical push or a direct insistence to make someone act.

2. "Press" also means to insist persistently and forcefully with someone to obtain something. Esau initially refuses Jacob's gift, but Jacob "insisted" with him (Genesis 33:11) until he accepted it. Samson's father-in-law "presses" the husband to stay one more night (Judges 19:7) — it is a repeated and insistent request.

3. The word can express violent or harassing pressure: in Genesis 19:9, the men of Sodom "press" Lot violently, aggressively pushing him toward the door. Here it is a brutal and threatening push.

4. In the moral and spiritual register, the word denotes arrogance or insolence — an attitude of presumption and disdain towards others or towards God. In 1 Samuel 15:23, "rebellion" against God (showing insolence towards Him) is compared to idolatry.
H6484.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּצַר comes from a root that evokes the action of pushing, forcing, pressing. The word belongs to a family of terms that speak of movement and physical pressure. The initial image is that of someone pushing against resistance — whether it be an object, a door, or a person's will. This image then generalizes to any form of insistence, forced perseverance, and even arrogance, which is a kind of moral push against the established order.
H6484.emploi: The verb appears about seven times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first used in the concrete sense: Lot "presses" his guests to enter his home (Genesis 19:3), instructs to "press" long to explore the land (2 Kings 2:17). Then it takes on the meaning of "insisting with" someone to obtain or refuse something: Jacob insists with Esau, the father-in-law insists with Samson's husband. The verb can also denote violent and hostile pressure: the men of Sodom "press" Lot brutally. Finally, in an ethical or religious context, it denotes arrogance or insolence towards God or others, as in 1 Samuel 15:23 where "rebelling" against God is called a form of insolence.
H6484.portee: This word shows us how insistence, when just and benevolent, can be a virtue — Lot welcomes his guests, Jacob generously offers. But it also warns us of the danger of pressuring, of that attitude which refuses to listen and imposes itself by force or pride. Insolence towards God is refusing to submit to His word, which is as serious as idolatry. The word thus invites us to discern between humble and persevering insistence, which honors God and others, and arrogance that destroys.

sens: counting people in a group, registering them on a list
reviewing an army, an organized group to know its strength
inquiring about someone, seeking to find them
watching over someone, taking care of them
punishing someone, holding them accountable for their actions
entrusting someone with the care of something
H6485A.detail: 1. Counting people in a group, registering them on a list: this is the fundamental, concrete, and administrative meaning of the word. A count is made to know the exact number of people and to create a list. Exodus 30:12 speaks of the counting of the children of Israel, each required to pay a ransom. 2. Reviewing an army, an organized group to know its strength: in a military or administrative context, men available for service or war are counted. Numbers 1:39 lists the men of the tribe of Dan who were counted. 3. Inquiring about someone, seeking to find them: the word can mean going in search of someone or checking their presence. Judges 21:9 recounts that the people were counted to verify that no inhabitant of Jabesh in Gilead was present. 4. Watching over someone, taking care of them: the word takes on a nuance of protective oversight, of particular attention given to someone. 5. Punishing someone, holding them accountable for their actions: the counting can become a punitive visit, where God holds each accountable for their actions. 6. Entrusting someone with the care of something: in this sense, it means appointing someone responsible for a charge or deposit.
H6485A.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "paying attention to" or "reviewing." Originally, it involves the action of looking carefully, examining, which naturally leads to counting and verifying presence. The root appears in several forms: the Niphal expresses passivity (being counted, being visited), while the Hiphil reinforces the idea of appointment or charge deposit. The word carries the image of a leader or administrator examining their troop or domain to ensure everything is accounted for.
H6485A.emploi: This verb appears 109 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the books of Exodus and Numbers, where the counts of Israel are a central theme. Its usage varies according to context: administrative (counting the tribes, the Levites), military (reviewing the armies), or religious (payment of ransom during the counting). The book of Numbers especially shows how the word becomes technical to designate the official operation of counting the community. The word can also refer to God's visit — a visit of blessing or punishment — which expands its meaning from "examining" to "judging" or "caring for." In Exodus 30:12-14, each counted man must pay a ransom, showing that the counting is never neutral: it is an act with religious consequences.
H6485A.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on each person's place in the people of God. The counting is not a mere administrative tally, but a recognition of each person's value before God. Everyone has a name, a place, a responsibility. Furthermore, the idea of "visitation" (God's visit to punish or bless) reminds us that God knows each by name and takes our actions into account. Finally, the word evokes the trust that God places in those He appoints to responsibilities: He "weighs" them and "deposits" them in the hands of others, as a sacred responsibility.

sens: meticulous inventory of objects or expenses
calculation of amounts spent or received
ordered enumeration of goods or materials
H6485B.detail:
1. The word refers to a detailed inventory, a precise record of what exists or what has been used. In Exodus 38:21, it is the account of the tabernacle: all the materials (gold, silver, bronze, wood, fabrics) that were used for the construction of the sanctuary are meticulously listed and verified.
2. This account involves verification, a check: each item is counted to ensure that none is missing and that everything has been used according to the orders received. Moses orders this work, entrusted to the Levites, to ensure that the management of sacred goods is transparent and above reproach.
H6485B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root פקד (paqad), which means "to count," "to verify," "to put in order." This root evokes the idea of reviewing, of taking inventory. It is also found in contexts of inspection (an officer tasked with counting the men of an army, for example) or benevolent oversight. The word פְּקוּדִים is the plural form, emphasizing that there are multiple counts or several items to enumerate.
H6485B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 38:21. It occurs when Moses has a complete inventory of the materials for the tabernacle made, after the construction is completed. It is both an administrative and religious act: the Levites, under the supervision of Ithamar (son of the high priest Aaron), are tasked with this verification. This context shows that the account is not mere arithmetic, but an act of faithfulness to God and a respect for the orders given.
H6485B.portee: This passage teaches that in the house of God, order, precision, and transparency matter. The goods intended for worship are not treated lightly: they are counted, verified, documented. For the believer, this underscores the importance of integrity in managing what has been entrusted to us, and the responsibility to God in both small details and large matters.

sens: Exercer un jugement, une sanction contre quelqu'un qui a commis une faute
Faire du tort à quelqu'un, le frapper, lui infliger un dommage
Prêter attention à, observer, veiller sur
Vérifier, passer en revue, compter ou énumérer
Visiter quelqu'un pour prendre soin de lui
H6485H.detail:
1. Châtier signifie d'abord punir, c'est-à-dire exercer un jugement divin contre ceux qui ont commis le mal. C'est un acte de justice : Dieu « châtiera tous les circoncis qui ne le sont pas de cœur » (Jeremiah 9:25), il « punira leurs péchés » (Hosea 8:13). C'est l'action d'un Juge qui rend justice en réponse au péché.
2. Le mot peut aussi signifier frapper, causer du dommage ou de la souffrance. C'est l'effet concret de la punition : la terre sera frappée par le jugement, les nations subiront les conséquences de leur culpabilité (Isaiah 26:21).
3. Châtier inclut l'idée de prêter attention, d'observer attentivement : Dieu « se souvient de leur iniquité » avant d'agir (Hosea 8:13), il remarque chaque infraction.
4. Le mot désigne aussi le fait de passer quelque chose en revue, de compter ou de numéroter — comme on inspecte les troupes ou on fait l'inventaire des dégâts. C'est une étape du jugement : d'abord vérifier, puis sanctionner.
5. Plus largement, c'est prendre soin de quelqu'un, le visiter, lui rendre visite — ce qui rappelle que derrière la punition se cache une relation : Dieu ne sort de sa demeure que parce qu'il a remarqué le mal chez son peuple (Isaiah 26:21).
H6485H.origine: Le verbe hébreu פָּקַד vient d'une racine primitive qui signifie « fixer l'attention sur », « diriger son regard vers ». Le mot exprime d'abord l'idée de s'intéresser à quelque chose, de la surveiller, d'en prendre soin. De là naît l'idée de commander, d'ordonner, de nommer quelqu'un à une fonction — on le « confie » une charge. La punition en découle naturellement : c'est faire tomber sur quelqu'un l'attention de la justice divine. Ainsi le mot oscille entre soin bienveillant et jugement sévère, selon le contexte.
H6485H.emploi: Le verbe פָּקַד apparaît 48 fois dans l'Ancien Testament, surtout chez les prophètes Jérémie (21 occurrences), Ésaïe, Osée et Amos. Dans la Segond, il se traduit par « châtier » ou « punir » dans environ 45 cas, et occasionnellement par « frapper ». Son emploi se concentre sur deux domaines : d'une part, l'annonce des châtiments de Dieu contre le peuple d'Israël et contre les nations (Jeremiah 5:9, 9:25, Hosea 8:13), d'autre part, les promesses de jugement futur (Isaiah 24:21 — Dieu « punira » les rois de la terre et l'armée d'en haut). Dans quelques versets rares (Job 35:15, Psalms 59:6, Amos 3:2), il prend le sens plus large d'« observer », de « prêter attention ». La tonalité est toujours celle du jugement divin : c'est Dieu qui châtie, jamais l'homme.
H6485H.portee: Ce mot rappelle au lecteur que la justice divine est active et minutieuse : Dieu ne ignore aucun péché, il remarque chaque faute. Mais il souligne aussi que Dieu agit après observation — il ne juge pas à la légère, mais en connaissance de cause. Pour le croyant, cela doit inspirer à la fois la crainte du jugement et la confiance en une justice vraie et équitable. La punition n'est jamais arbitraire : elle répond à une faute précise, observée et comptabilisée.

sens: Se rendre auprès de quelqu'un pour voir comment il va, pour l'inspecter ou le compter
Se souvenir de quelqu'un, avoir quelqu'un en pensée, s'occuper de lui
Punir quelqu'un pour ses fautes, exercer une rétribution
Confier à quelqu'un la charge de surveiller, de diriger
Constater l'absence ou le manque de quelque chose
H6485I.detail:
1. Visiter signifie d'abord aller voir quelqu'un ou quelque chose pour l'examiner : c'est se présenter devant lui et le regarder attentivement. Quand l'Éternel « visite » Noé (Genesis 50:25), il le voit pour vérifier son état ; quand un guerrier « visite » le camp ennemi, il l'inspecte pour en faire le compte.

2. Visiter veut dire aussi se souvenir avec soin de quelqu'un, le tenir dans son cœur et agir pour lui. Quand l'Éternel « se souvient » de Sara, il ne s'agit pas d'un simple souvenir oublieux : il s'occupe d'elle avec intention et réalise sa promesse (Genesis 21:1). C'est une pensée qui produit une action.

3. Visiter quelqu'un ou ses fautes, c'est aussi le punir, le châtier pour ses iniquités : l'Éternel « punit » l'iniquité des pères sur les enfants (Exodus 20:5). La visite devient alors une rétribution, une conséquence de la transgression.

4. Visiter peut aussi signifier établir quelqu'un sur une charge, lui confier la responsabilité de surveiller et de diriger. C'est mettre un berger sur les brebis ou un intendant sur une maison.

5. Visiter exprime enfin le fait de constater l'absence ou le manque de quelqu'un : chercher quelqu'un et le « trouver manquant », « avoir besoin » de lui, c'est remarquer qu'il n'est plus là.
H6485I.origine: La racine פקד exprime l'idée fondamentale d'une attention soutenue et d'un mouvement de vérification. Elle est apparentée à des mots qui signifient « examiner », « regarder de près ». L'image de départ est celle de quelqu'un qui « se tourne vers », qui « vient regarder ». Cette racine produit aussi des mots pour « visite », « garde », « intendance ». Dans l'Ancien Testament grec, le verbe grec ἐπισκέπτομαι (episképtomai) traduit souvent ce verbe hébreu, renforçant l'idée de regard attentif et de sollicitude.
H6485I.emploi: Ce verbe apparaît environ 40 fois dans l'Ancien Testament. Il est fréquent dans la Genèse (patriarches), l'Exode (action de l'Éternel envers Israël), les Psaumes (prières de demande de visite divine), et chez les Prophètes (visitation du jugement). Ses emplois varient selon le contexte : visiter au sens de « venir voir » (Judges 15:1), visiter au sens de « se souvenir » et agir (Genesis 21:1 — l'Éternel et Sara ; Exodus 4:31 — le peuple se souvenait de la parole), visiter au sens de « punir » (Exodus 20:5, 32:34 — châtiment des iniquités), visiter au sens de « compter » ou « passer en revue » un peuple (Exodus 30:12 — dénombrement), visiter au sens de « confier une charge » (Jeremiah 23:2 — bergers préposés). Un même passage peut combiner plusieurs sens.
H6485I.portee: Ce verbe révèle comment Dieu se rapporte à son peuple : non pas comme un absent ou un indifférent, mais comme celui qui « visite » — qui regarde, se souvient, intervient et demande des comptes. Pour le croyant, « être visité » par l'Éternel est à la fois réconfort (il ne nous oublie pas) et avertissement (ses yeux sont sur nous). Ce mot appelle à la conscience morale : nos actes sont comptés, remarqués, et auront des conséquences. Il invite aussi le croyant à imiter cette attention vigilante envers les autres.

sens: Appoint someone to a position, place them in charge of a function or group
Hand something over to someone for them to be responsible for, entrust it to their care
Count, enumerate, conduct an inspection of
Examine, look closely, pay attention to
Punish, strike, inflict correction
Visit, be concerned about someone's situation
H6485J.detail:
